Partisan Banks and Creditor Coordination Within Loan Syndicates
papers.abstract: We investigate how firm‐level partisanship influences interactions between banks in the syndicated loan market. Because politically divergent banks hold conflicting perceptions of economic conditions, ideological distance between banks impedes consensus and elevates expected coordination costs. We find that greater political distance between a lead arranger and a participant reduces the participant's likelihood of joining a syndicate and lowers its retained loan share relative to the lead. The relation between political distance and loan share differences intensifies during periods of high national political polarization. Moreover, greater political diversity within a syndicate is associated with less restrictive loan covenants and higher interest spreads, reflecting a trade‐off where lenders sacrifice contingent control to avoid costly renegotiation gridlock. Validating our disagreement mechanism, we show that following presidential elections, banks politically misaligned with the incoming administration issue significantly more pessimistic macroeconomic forecasts than aligned banks.

papers.title: The Role of Supply Chains in Climate Disclosure
papers.abstract: We examine the role of supply chains in shaping the public disclosure of climate information. We leverage a unique empirical setting enabled by CDP—the leading platform for corporate climate risk reporting—which allows customers to demand climate‐related information from their suppliers. Using a large international sample of customer–supplier pairs, we find a positive association between customers’ information demand and suppliers’ public disclosure on the CDP. While the estimated association is modest on average, it exhibits substantial cross‐sectional variation reflecting the disclosure incentives of both customers and suppliers as well as their relative bargaining power. We also find descriptive evidence consistent with one potential implication of the documented association for corporate decision‐making: shifts in supply network relationships toward greener and more transparent suppliers. Overall, our findings contribute to ongoing debates on how to foster climate disclosure.

papers.title: The Anti‐SLAPP Statutes and Corporate Environmental Policies
papers.abstract: We examine whether legal protection for civic participation affects corporate pollution. Polluters may deter public discipline through strategic lawsuits. Anti‐SLAPP (Strategic Lawsuit Against Public Participation) statutes mitigate this threat by enabling prompt dismissal and recovery of legal costs. Using a difference‐in‐differences design, we find that enacting an anti‐SLAPP statute in a state significantly reduces toxic emissions from that state by increasing local public pressure. The reduction is greater when the statutes provide stronger protection, when local stakeholders have stronger incentives and abilities to discipline polluters, and when local public pressure increases more after the enactment. Plants lower emissions by improving abatement rather than by reducing output or relocating emissions. Our paper underscores the role of legal protection in environmental governance and informs policy debates over anti‐SLAPP legislation.

papers.title: National Audit Oversight and Foreign Investment
papers.abstract: Public audit oversight bodies have become ubiquitous following the establishment of the U.S. PCAOB in 2002. However, despite their cost and prominence, little is known of their economic implications, if any. We examine the relation between establishment of public audit oversight bodies (POBs) and cross-border investment. Using a difference-in-differences design, we find that after a country establishes a POB, the country attracts more foreign capital. Our results suggest that total foreign portfolio investment (FPI) increases by approximately $11 billion for the average country that establishes a POB. The impact of POBs on foreign investment is dependent on the effectiveness of the POB in improving audit quality and the strength of a country’s existing institutional environment. Our study provides evidence of real economic effects of public audit oversight around the world, which adds to the literature on auditor oversight and to the broader literature on economic consequences of regulation. Data Availability: Data are available from the public sources cited in the text. JEL Classifications: M42; M48; F21; L51; G15; G18.

papers.title: The Cost of Regulatory Inaction: Evidence from IFRS Nonadoption
papers.abstract: Although extensive research examines the costs and benefits of adopting new disclosure regulations, little addresses the consequences of regulatory inaction. We investigate whether firms in nonadopting countries incur additional information losses, beyond the forgone benefits, when their foreign peers adopt International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS). Nonadopters bear an absolute liquidity cost as foreign peers adopt IFRS, consistent with negative externalities from IFRS and accompanying reforms. Exploiting heterogeneity across nonadopting countries, we observe more pronounced liquidity declines among firms with greater institutional ownership overlap with IFRS peers. This effect appears more pronounced when IFRS peers are domiciled in countries with concurrent enforcement reforms or greater comparability improvements. Further evidence shows shared intermediaries—investors and analysts—reduce information production for nonadopters as other firms in their portfolios adopt IFRS. Overall, regulatory inaction degrades information environments: resources shift to the new regime, worsening liquidity for firms in the old regime. Data Availability: Data used in this study are available from commercial sources cited in the text. JEL Classifications: G1; K22; M41; M48.

papers.title: Board–CEO Trust and Concealing Adverse News
papers.abstract: We investigate how generalized trust, a culturally rooted belief in the trustworthiness of unfamiliar others, influences board oversight. Using an ancestry-based measure of board–CEO trust based on ancestral origins and bilateral trust scores across countries, we find a significant positive relation between board–CEO trust and stock price crash risk, indicating higher bad-news hoarding. This relation remains robust across alternative crash risk measures, sample specifications, and trust measures. Firms with high board–CEO trust exhibit more asymmetric stock market reactions to good news versus bad news and a higher likelihood of material restatements. Analyses of insider trading patterns show that directors in high-trust firms are less informed than CEOs about adverse developments, supporting lax board monitoring rather than collusion between directors and CEOs. Overall, the evidence suggests that culturally inherited trust can weaken board oversight and reduce corporate transparency, consistent with an underexplored governance friction even within well-structured boards. Data Availability: Data used in this study are available from public sources identified in the study. JEL Classifications: G14; G34; G41; M12.

papers.title: Private Firm Disclosures and Public Firms' Debt Choice
papers.abstract: Analyzing a cross-country sample, we provide evidence implying that private firm disclosure transparency narrows information asymmetry, which, in turn, lowers public firms' reliance on bank debt. Channel tests help substantiate that private firm disclosure elicits this positive externality, evident in lower monitoring demand, lower borrowing costs, and higher credit rating quality. Cross-sectional results suggest that the impact of private firm transparency is larger when public firms suffer worse information opacity, private firm disclosures are more important to their public peers, and bond markets are more developed. In relying on the staggered implementation of electronic business registers as a plausibly exogenous shock and a simulated disclosure scope as the instrumental variable, we continue to find that private firm disclosures reduce public firms' bank debt reliance, helping to alleviate endogeneity threats. Data Availability Statement: The data used in this study are obtained from publicly available sources identified in the paper. JEL Classifications: G32; G21; M41.

papers.title: Target Firm Material Contract Redactions and Valuation in Acquisitions
papers.abstract: We study whether and how the SEC’s confidential treatment program, which allows firms to redact proprietary information from material contracts, affects valuation in corporate acquisitions. We find that friendly acquisitions of redacting targets generate significantly higher positive announcement returns for both targets and acquirers compared with acquisitions of nonredacting targets. These positive returns are also more pronounced when targets are likelier to hold valuable proprietary information. In addition, friendly acquisitions of redacting targets achieve better long-term performance and recognize fewer subsequent goodwill impairments compared with acquisitions of nonredacting targets. Our findings of a robust association between target firm material contract redactions and target and acquirer announcement returns are consistent with a dual disclosure perspective, whereby redaction preserves target proprietary value, which is transferred privately to the acquirer through due diligence. Data Availability: Data are available from public sources identified in the paper; some require a subscription. JEL Classifications: D8; M41; M48.

papers.title: The Effect of Cost Elasticity Choice on Loss Reversal
papers.abstract: Although the prevalence of losses has been increasing over the years, little is known about how managerial decisions lead to reversing losses back to profits. We find cost elasticity choices, implied by operating actions made in advance, significantly increase the likelihood of loss reversal. We show loss firms with high cost elasticity exhibit significantly higher long-term survival rates and are therefore less likely to exercise the abandonment option than loss firms with low cost elasticity. The contributions are twofold. First, the findings shed light on a mechanism underlying loss reversal. We extend the loss literature by promoting the understanding of how ex ante cost elasticity choices affect the likelihood of loss reversal. Second, the findings enrich the cost accounting literature by demonstrating a unique performance implication of a cost elasticity choice. Data Availability: The data used in this study are obtained from third-party subscription databases, Compustat and CRSP, as described in the text. JEL Classifications: M41.

papers.title: Rational Information Acquisition Screens
papers.abstract: We develop and empirically test a model of information acquisition in capital markets. In the model, investors are uncertain about the returns to acquiring private information before they acquire it. This results in a novel reason for why past price movements affect future capital market outcomes: investors use public information, including past prices, as a screen to estimate the returns to acquiring private information and efficiently allocate their limited information-processing capacity across firms. The model predicts that larger unexplained price movements lead to more private information acquisition, higher future price volatility, and higher future expected trading volume. Using fine-grained data measuring information acquisition on EDGAR and Bloomberg, we provide empirical evidence in support of the model’s predictions. Data Availability: All data are available from the sources cited in the text. JEL Classifications: D83; G12; G14; M41.

papers.title: Environmental, Social, and Governance Ratings of Environmental, Social, and Governance Index Providers
papers.abstract: We explore the role of ESG raters’ business models in the production of their ratings, noting that increasingly ESG raters not only produce ESG ratings but also construct and sell ESG indices. We examine whether index licensing incentives are associated with how ESG ratings relate to stock returns. By comparing ratings across raters for the same firm, we control for fundamental ESG performance. We find that raters with strong index licensing incentives assign higher ESG ratings to firms with better stock performance compared to raters with weaker licensing incentives, and that this association is concentrated among index-eligible firms. We further show that index construction is significantly associated with stock returns, and that the high-incentive rater adjusts its ratings following index composition changes, whereas the low-incentive rater does not. Our findings highlight the need for greater transparency in the incentives of ESG rating producers. JEL Classifications: G24; M14; M40; M41; M48; Q56.

papers.title: The Impact of Mandatory Audit Firm Rotation on Competitive Pricing Strategies for New Audit Engagements: Evidence From the European Union
papers.abstract: Mandatory audit firm rotation was introduced in the European Union (EU), in part, to make the audit market more dynamic by bringing audit engagements to market more frequently. However, it creates a countervailing economic force: By limiting the duration of auditor–client relationships, mandatory rotation shortens the period over which auditors can recoup first‐year fee discounts through fees earned in subsequent years. Consistent with this argument, we find that first‐year fee discounts decline substantially after mandatory firm rotation took effect in the EU, particularly in countries with stricter limits on auditor tenure. Thus, greater opportunities to compete for new engagements do not necessarily translate into greater first‐year fee discounts. Our findings highlight that regulators should consider not only how frequently audit engagements are brought to market but also how limits on auditor tenure shape the pricing incentives associated with competing for new clients.

papers.title: Intertemporal Dynamics of Cost Asymmetry
papers.abstract: We study the intertemporal dynamics of asymmetric cost behavior in a competitive setting. Our analysis delves into the primitives of cost asymmetry and explores its dynamic evolution over time. The analysis yields the result that cost behavior is asymmetric by default and path‐dependent, transpiring as cost stickiness following prior resource expansion and taking the form of cost anti‐stickiness after previous resource contraction. The analysis further suggests that the magnitude of cost asymmetry, either stickiness or anti‐stickiness, is decreasing in demand uncertainty and competition intensity, increasing in adjustment costs and time discounting, and greater for small demand shocks than for large demand shocks. By highlighting cost asymmetry as a dynamic, rather than static, phenomenon, and by providing new, testable predictions regarding the direction and magnitude of cost asymmetry across firms and over time, our results offer theoretical grounding for the empirical cost asymmetry literature and may also help investors and other stakeholders interpret cost behavior in light of firms' recent history of expansion or contraction and their competitive environment.

papers.title: The Effect of Non‐US Tax Authority Monitoring on Income Shifting by Affiliates of US Multinationals: Evidence From EDGAR Search Activity
papers.abstract: Governments worldwide are concerned that multinational enterprises (MNEs) shift profits across borders to avoid taxes. While prior research shows that home‐country tax enforcement can reduce tax avoidance, far less is known about whether foreign tax authorities (FTAs) can constrain income shifting by MNE affiliates. We measure FTA monitoring using data on FTAs' downloads of US MNEs' annual reports filed with the SEC. We find that FTA monitoring is more intensive in higher‐tax‐rate countries with a larger MNE presence, consistent with those jurisdictions facing stronger incentives to monitor income shifting. More importantly, we find that monitoring by an affiliate's local tax authority does not systematically reduce income shifting by US MNE affiliates, whereas aggregate monitoring in the MNE group affects an affiliate even when its own local FTA is not observably monitoring it. This result is consistent with a spillover effect of FTA monitoring. This association is stronger when FTAs operate under information‐exchange treaties, when company disclosures are more detailed, and when enforcement capacity is greater. We also find positive associations between aggregate FTA monitoring and subsequent tax avoidance and tax settlements of US MNEs. Our findings suggest monitoring by multiple FTAs effectively combats MNE tax avoidance and have implications for how tax administrations design and coordinate monitoring efforts.

papers.title: Using Financial Accounting Information to Estimate the Income Shifting of US Multinationals
papers.abstract: Existing estimates of how much income US multinational corporations (MNCs) shift out of the United States differ dramatically, and most cannot identify which specific firms do the shifting. We use data from firms' public financial reports to derive firm‐year estimates of US MNCs' outbound income shifting. We find that aggregate US outbound income shifting is substantially lower than widely cited macroeconomic‐based estimates, with the gap driven primarily by double counting of foreign income in macroeconomic data rather than by differences in firms' sensitivity to tax rates. Income shifting is also highly concentrated among a small number of firms, primarily in intangible‐intensive industries such as computers and pharmaceuticals, while most MNCs shift little or no income. This concentration implies that size‐based thresholds embedded in the OECD's Pillar 2 and the US corporate alternative minimum tax will capture the most active income shifters but may also impose compliance burdens on many firms that shift minimal income. These findings have direct implications for policy‐makers designing international tax rules, tax authorities prioritizing audit resources toward high‐risk income shifters, and investors and lenders assessing MNCs' tax‐related exposures.

papers.title: Mandatory Disclosure and Peer Firms' Learning From Stock Prices
papers.abstract: Theory posits that mandatory disclosure influences peer firms' learning from stock prices in two non‐mutually exclusive ways: intra‐industry information transfers and the reallocation of information acquisition efforts. Using mandatory segment disclosure as our setting, we document a decrease in investment‐ q sensitivity for peers of disclosing firms. This effect is stronger among peers with greater economic links to disclosing firms and peers with the greatest incentives to glean information from prices. Our findings provide novel evidence that mandatory disclosure can have significant negative externalities on peer firms' investment efficiency via a managerial learning from the stock price channel. These insights inform regulators assessing the economic consequences of mandatory disclosure, while also assisting managers who rely on information from stock prices to guide investment decisions.

papers.title: Whose Job Is It, Anyway? The Effect of the Review Process on Employee Performance
papers.abstract: Companies have widely adopted a system of work‐product reviews whereby the work of one individual is subsequently reviewed by another to ensure its quality. We examine how managers can effectively implement a review of employee work to improve performance. Organizations review employees' work to identify mistakes and improve work quality. However, reviews may also reduce employees' effort and initiative if they expect reviewers to identify and correct their errors for them. We use an experiment to examine how employee performance depends on who conducts the review and how feedback is provided. Specifically, participants' work was reviewed by either a superior or a peer, and the reviewer provided either general, high‐level guidance (autonomy‐oriented) or specific corrective information about errors (dependency‐oriented). Employees performed best when superiors provided high‐level guidance or when peers provided specific corrective feedback, with these benefits emerging over time. Guidance from a superior increased employees' sense of responsibility, whereas corrective help from a peer strengthened feelings of teamwork and cohesion. Review approaches that did not fit these combinations offered no clear performance benefit relative to having no review. The findings show that review effectiveness depends on matching the feedback approach to the reviewer's organizational rank. These results have important implications for managers, accountants responsible for internal controls, and audit professionals involved in designing and implementing the review process.

papers.title: XBRL adoption and SEC monitoring
papers.abstract: We examine how disclosure processing costs influence SEC monitoring of firm disclosures by leveraging the mandatory adoption of XBRL—a digital reporting language designed to reduce these costs. Post adoption, both the frequency and quality of SEC comment letters for 10-K filings increase. Additional tests suggest that XBRL enhances SEC monitoring through three channels. First, automated data extraction improves review efficiency, as reflected in more timely comment letters and greater XBRL benefits when the SEC faces tighter resource constraints or uses XBRL analytical tools. Second, standardized reporting strengthens the SEC’s benchmarking ability: firms using more standardized tags and tags more comparable to those of industry peers benefit more. Third, XBRL facilitates SEC scrutiny of complex reporting issues, yielding more frequent and higher-quality comments on noncore earnings accounts and for firms with more footnote tags or complex filings. Overall, our evidence suggests that reduced disclosure processing costs enhance the SEC’s regulatory monitoring.

Disclosing work-from-home flexibility to compete for talent? Evidence from job postings
papers.abstract: Job postings serve as one of the primary means to communicate with prospective employees, enabling employers to highlight the benefits of the position and attract qualified applicants. As work-from-home flexibility has become increasingly prevalent, this study examines whether employers strategically disclose work-from-home flexibility in their job postings and how this disclosure is associated with hiring outcomes. Using a comprehensive sample of job postings from US employers between 2017 and 2024, we find that employers are more likely to disclose work-from-home flexibility when facing greater labor market competition and that disclosing this flexibility is associated with a higher job vacancy filling rate, especially when work-from-home information is disclosed in a more salient manner. However, we document a positive association between work-from-home disclosures and subsequent employee turnover, suggesting potential costs associated with these disclosures. These findings add to the growing literature on firms’ strategic disclosure targeted towards labor markets.

Implementation of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals: selected case studies from Pakistan and Chile
papers.abstract: Purpose This study examines how global frameworks such as the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) are implemented at the individual company level and what role accounting and other calculative practices play in such processes. Design/methodology/approach Extensive fieldwork-based case studies are undertaken in Pakistan and Chile with multiple qualitative methods employed including documentary analysis, interviews and non-participant observations. Theorisation is grounded within the Saidian dialectic encompassing authority and molestation in relation to texts. Findings We observe that processes of SDG implementation by organisations are intertwined with molestation of the global goals, which are operationalisable by organisations. They are represented through processes of authorship subject to the dialectical relationship of authority and molestation within calculative practices. Research limitations/implications We extend Said's concepts of authority and molestation from the discourse to corporate practice, SDG implementation processes and accounting thereof, in an emerging economy context. Practical implications Practising managers face context-specific challenges involved in implementing SDG framework which was not originally designed for the organisational level implementation. Future iterations of SDGs, in whatever form they come, require organisation level implementation guidance based on national and cultural contexts. Originality/value This study departs from the tradition of previous SDG research, mainly conducted at the macro national level, to bring in more micro company-level insights. It extends the theoretical understanding of the dialectic nature of authority and molestation within organisational engagement with SDGs.

papers.title: Management consultants – monsters or benign change agents? The case of the NSW transport asset holding entity
papers.abstract: Purpose This study critically examines the role of private consultants in public-sector financial governance under New Public Management (NPM) and New Public Financial Management (NPFM). Focusing on the New South Wales Transport Asset Holding Entity (TAHE), the research investigates how consultancy expertise and accounting technologies were mobilised in the case study to construct a quasi-market entity that advanced short-term fiscal objectives while obscuring long-term financial realities and the public interest. Design/methodology/approach Grounded in political economy and public-interest accounting traditions, the study employs a multi-method, qualitative case study design. Informed by the theoretical lenses of consultocracy and consultology, the analysis triangulates legally vetted and publicly contested documents, including Auditor-General reports, parliamentary inquiries, financial disclosures and investigative journalism, to trace institutional decision-making and intra-firm knowledge practices. Findings The analysis demonstrates that consultants acted as powerful political-institutional actors. They shaped the structural and financial design of TAHE to classify capital funding as equity rather than as an expenditure. Crucially, distinct consultancy teams within a single Big Four firm produced contradictory asset valuations. Internal firm dynamics helped contain these contradictions, which included impression management, team segmentation and the disciplining of professional dissent. Together, they enabled the firm to suppress contradictory judgements, prioritising commercial and political imperatives over democratic accountability and public transparency. Originality/value This paper introduces consultology as a micro-analytic complement to consultocracy, showing how consultant power operates both institutionally and intra-firm through practices that stabilise contradictory expertise. The TAHE case reveals accounting classifications as political technologies that embed long-term fiscal obligations and accountability risks beyond effective oversight.

papers.title: Two limericks about ethics

Revisiting new accounting history four decades on: reconciling traditional and critical historiographies
papers.abstract: Purpose Revisiting debates in New Accounting History four decades on, this paper advances accounting historiography through the development of a Neo-Critical Accounting History (NCAH) framework that systematically integrates the strengths of traditional accounting history with the theoretically informed and critical orientation of new accounting history. In answering the “how” question, the framework offers an analytical pathway through which accounting historians may proceed with a rigorous and socially attuned mode of inquiry. Design/methodology/approach The study is grounded in critical accounting approach, in particular, Habermas's method of rational reconstruction (Held, 1980) providing the philosophical foundation for proposing an agenda advancing framework for NCAH. The framework integrates the methods of historical academic monograph with key features of both traditional and new accounting history. Findings The proposed NCAH framework is articulated across three interrelated dimensions. First, it integrates traditional and critical historiography by combining historical rigour with critical depth to recover marginalised voices and enhance contextual analysis. Second, it advances epistemic pluralisation through rigorous source critique, methodological triangulation, and engagement with diverse archival and counter-accounts, thereby addressing archival silences, partialities, and power relations. Third, it embraces theoretical openness and contemporary relevance, enabling historical inquiry into emerging accounting-related topics aligned with broader societal and ethical concerns, and strengthening accounting history's engagement with contemporary scholarly and public debates. Originality/value The manuscript demonstrates how traditional and new accounting history approaches may be systematically integrated, including through approaches inspired by abductive reasoning. Within this framing, narrative is positioned not as an end in itself, but rather as a point of departure for deeper theoretical interpretation and historical analysis. In doing so, NCAH reconciles historical and archival rigour with theoretical openness, thereby enhancing the analytical depth of the discipline and its capacity to contribute to interdisciplinary scholarship, societal reflection, and professional practice.

papers.title: Environmental accountability: avoidable methane and VOC contamination in Alberta’s oilpatch
papers.abstract: Purpose This study examines how the Alberta government’s October 2000 withdrawal of the Long-Term Inactive Well Program and its replacement with the Licensee Liability Rating system enabled two decades of avoidable methane and volatile organic compound (VOC) contamination. It analyzes how accounting-based regulatory choices, co-participation between government and corporations and the withholding of environmental information facilitated the indefinite deferral of decommissioning and reclamation, producing major environmental and health consequences. Design/methodology/approach A total of 7,380 pages of internal government records obtained through a series of freedom-of-information (FOI) requests were integrated with well-level production data for 599,002 Alberta wells covering 1961–2018. After extensive cleaning and organization, these materials were used to reconstruct regulatory decision-making and to generate tables and spatial mapping of cumulative contamination patterns. Our analyses qualitatively interpret the documentary evidence to illuminate the accounting-implicated regulatory choices that shaped Alberta’s non-producing well problem and their environmental consequences. Findings The LLR’s design – originating in a proposal authored by a Canadian Natural Resources Ltd. employee and using reclamation costs supplied by the Canadian Association of Petroleum Producers – shifted regulatory focus from the timely decommissioning of non-producing wells to the management of financial risk to the orphan fund. This shift enabled wells to remain undecommissioned for decades, generating an estimated 2.3 million well-years of avoidable contamination. By 2018, nearly 10% of Alberta’s landmass lay within 500 m of a non-producing undecommissioned well, including First Nations reserves that had few such wells three decades earlier, and the regulator’s own internal calculations indicate that the 15 largest oilpatch corporations would, at current rates, require an average of 288 years to decommission their existing inventories of inactive wells. Originality/value This study is the first to integrate FOI-obtained regulatory records with privately purchased well-level data to map the cumulative, avoidable environmental consequences of accounting-implicated regulatory changes. It contends that in co-participatory settings of resource extraction and environmental degradation, where governments and corporations are structurally aligned through royalty dependence, accounting academics can and should seek to uncover, analyze and publicize environmental information that governments and corporations prefer to keep hidden and to place such information into the hands of audiences capable of mobilizing it within accountability struggles.

papers.title: Accounting and the fragmented self: institutional opacity, spiritual inequality and moral burden in Islamic finance
papers.abstract: Purpose This study examines how Islamic financial institutions, despite claiming ethical legitimacy, may reproduce spiritual and moral inequalities. Drawing on Muhammad Iqbal's concept of khudi (Self), the study examines how institutional opacity, limited theological engagement and compliance-oriented practices displace moral responsibility onto individuals, forcing consumers to navigate financial choices amid guilt, uncertainty and fragmented ethical agency. Design/methodology/approach The study adopts a qualitative interpretive approach, drawing on 30 semi-structured interviews with UK-based Muslim consumers who currently hold or have previously held Islamic financial products. The data were analysed thematically to explore how individuals experience ethical ambiguity, self-surveillance and clerical authority, and how they resist the commodification of their faith within modern financial systems. Findings Rather than a transparent ethical alternative, Islamic finance asserts moral authority without substantive justification. Facing institutional opacity and limited theological reasoning, participants internalise moral risk through guilt and self-surveillance. This uneven clarity erodes trust in religious authority, intensifies spiritual disorientation, and exposes how institutions can privatise accountability while retaining institutional legitimacy. Research limitations/implications By introducing khudi as a counter-accountability framework to demonstrate that inequalities take spiritual and moral forms, the study offers a new ontological lens for reimagining accountability as a dialogical and emancipatory practice. It urges institutions, Shariah boards and standard-setters to move beyond formal, audit-driven compliance. It repositions accountability as a substantive ethical practice, demanding that claims of Islamic legitimacy be structurally transparent and publicly justified. Originality/value Extending critical accounting scholarship, the study reveals that inequality in Islamic finance is spiritual and moral. By introducing Iqbal's khudi (Self), it provides a novel framework demonstrating how calculative regimes can either fragment or sustain the transcendent Self, repositioning accountability as a site for reclaiming spiritual agency.

papers.title: Binding the present and orchestrating the future: accounting as a technology of government in water sustainability
papers.abstract: Purpose The paper explains how water sustainability becomes governable in fragmented hybrid settings. It shows how accounting and accountability hold together diverse actors, competing obligations and different rationalities, enabling sustainability aspirations to translate into coordinated action. The paper illuminates the fragile character of this process, showing how accounting and accountability partially stabilise tensions without resolving them. Design/methodology/approach The study adopts an interpretive case study of an Italian water utility undergoing regulatory and organisational changes. It applies Dean's analytics of government framework to analyse data from interviews, sustainability reports and publicly available documents. Findings The study identifies four regimes of practice through which water sustainability was rendered governable. Across these regimes, accounting and accountability perform “binding” and “orchestrating” roles in governing water sustainability. These practices establish norms, responsibilities and incentives (binding) and align actors and activities (orchestrating), thereby stabilising but not resolving inter-regime tensions. Practical implications The study helps multiple actors, such as managers, policymakers and stakeholders, to understand how accounting and accountability can support the organisation of collective responsibility for water sustainability. Social implications The study shows how accounting and accountability redistribute responsibility for water sustainability across organisations and communities in hybrid public–private settings. In doing so, they can promote collective responsibility for water conservation but may also normalise particular ways of valuing water. Originality/value The paper introduces the concepts of binding and orchestrating to explain how accounting and accountability render sustainability governable in fragmented hybrid settings. Its value lies in showing how accounting enables collective action while leaving unresolved tensions among economic, public-service and environmental commitments visible.

papers.title: Constructing sustainability expertise: capital conversion and the making of a sustainability CFO
papers.abstract: Purpose This paper examines how a Chief Financial Officer (CFO) in a Sri Lankan state-owned bank constructed sustainability accounting as a new domain of professional expertise. Extending Baxter and Chua's (2008) conception of accounting expertise as an organisational accomplishment, the paper asks how entirely new forms of accounting expertise are constructed before organisational legitimacy, evaluative criteria and professional jurisdiction have been established, drawing on Bourdieu's theory of field, habitus and capital to explain this process. Design/methodology/approach The study uses a longitudinal qualitative case study of a CFO in a Sri Lankan state-owned housing bank, whose sustainability agenda developed during the country's post-tsunami reconstruction. Data were collected across two phases (2013–2014) using 44 semi-structured interviews with 25 participants, supplemented by field notes and documentary analysis of sustainability reports, policy documents and media coverage. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis, proceeding from inductive coding through temporal coding to theoretical interpretation via Baxter and Chua (2008) and Bourdieu, tracing the sequential conversion of cultural, symbolic, social and positional capital. Findings Sustainability accounting expertise was constructed through a cumulative process of capital conversion. An entrepreneurial habitus generated the disposition to recognise emerging opportunities, enabling the accumulation of cultural capital through learning, authorship and reporting innovation. This cultural capital was converted into symbolic capital through managerial endorsement and award recognition, which expanded social capital through strategic alliances, and was ultimately converted into positional authority, redefining the finance function's organisational jurisdiction. However, this expertise construction did not automatically translate into institutionalisation: sustainability expertise remained concentrated in a single individual rather than becoming embedded in organisational systems and routines. Research limitations/implications The single-case design prioritises theoretical development over statistical generalisation; future research should examine whether similar processes of expertise construction occur across different organisational, professional and national settings. The case also centres on an unusually entrepreneurial CFO, and alternative trajectories may emerge where sustainability initiatives are collectively led or externally mandated. The longitudinal design captured the construction of expertise but not its longer-term reproduction following leadership succession, pointing to a need for future research on how such expertise diffuses, evolves or declines once its original architect departs the organisation. Practical implications Organisations should not equate the success of a prominent sustainability champion with the institutionalisation of sustainability capability. Individual actors can mobilise resources, secure legitimacy and accelerate organisational innovation, but sustained transformation depends on converting individually held expertise into collective organisational capability. Building durable sustainability capacity therefore requires deliberate investment in knowledge sharing, succession planning and cross-functional learning, alongside organisational systems that embed expertise beyond the individual who originally constructed it, reducing organisations' dependence on any single actor for the continuity of their sustainability agenda. Originality/value The paper offers a distinctive contribution by reconceptualising accounting expertise as something that must first be constructed, rather than simply organisationally accomplished, in emerging domains such as sustainability accounting. By integrating Bourdieu's theory of field, habitus and capital with Baxter and Chua's (2008) framework, it identifies cumulative capital conversion as the specific social mechanism underlying this process – a mechanism not previously articulated in the sustainability accounting literature. It further offers the original insight that expertise construction and organisational institutionalisation are analytically distinct, showing that individually constructed expertise can achieve legitimacy while remaining fragile and undiffused across the organisation.

papers.journal: Auditing: A Journal of Practice and Theory
papers.title: Does Releasing Earnings When the Audit Is Less Complete Increase Audit Costs?
papers.abstract: Annual earnings announcements (EAs) are a key information source for capital market participants. Because the value of EAs is largely driven by their timeliness, many companies issue EAs before the annual audit is complete. Building on prior findings that releasing earnings prior to audit completion is associated with increased risk, we examine the association between early EAs and audit fees. We find that companies that release earnings before audit completion pay a fee premium of 10.8 percent, on average. This premium increases with the number of days between the EA and audit report dates and is generalizable across many auditor and engagement characteristics. Using a changes analysis, we also document that the increase in audit fees persists for at least two years after clients shift to early EAs. Our results provide important evidence of a direct financial cost of releasing earnings before auditors have completed their year-end fieldwork. Data Availability: Data are available from the public sources cited in the text. JEL Classifications: G33; M4; M42.

papers.journal: Auditing: A Journal of Practice and Theory
papers.title: Audit Team Research: A Systematic Review of the Literature and Directions for Future Research
papers.abstract: An audit team encompasses members of the audit engagement team and other individuals within or contracted by the firm whose actions can directly influence audit outcomes. Research on audit teams has gained increasing attention over the past decade. We systematically review the audit team literature from this period across all methodological approaches. Leveraging a theoretical framework from organizational behavior, we classify audit research under the topics of audit teams' compositional inputs, structural inputs, and mediating mechanisms (processes and emergent states) that convert inputs to outcomes. Research on compositional inputs examines staff allocation and involvement, team diversity, knowledge, and continuity. Studies of structural inputs cover group audits, joint audits, national office consultations, offshoring, and multiple team memberships. Research on mediating mechanisms examines transition, action, and interpersonal processes and team cognition and affect. We highlight key takeaways and propose future research avenues. Data Availability: The data used in this study are available from the sources described in the manuscript. JEL Classifications: M41; M42.

papers.journal: Auditing: A Journal of Practice and Theory
papers.title: Alternative Data as Audit Risk Signals: Evidence from Online-Sales Data
papers.abstract: We examine whether the availability of alternative data affects audit outcomes. Using the introduction of online-sales data by Wind, a major financial data provider in China, we find that third-party online-sales information is associated with improved revenue reporting quality. To capture cross-sectional variation, we construct a Book-to-Wind sales discrepancy index (BWI) that measures the divergence between reported sales growth and externally observed online-sales growth. The effects on revenue reporting quality are stronger for firms with higher BWI and clients audited by non-Big 10 or nonindustry-specialist auditors. Audit fees decrease on average. Notably, audit fees increase for high-BWI firms and decrease for low-BWI firms, consistent with the risk-based reallocation of audit effort. Overall, our findings provide early evidence that online-sales signals function as audit-relevant risk indicators that enhance the rigor of revenue-focused audits. Data Availability: The data used in this study are available from the sources identified in the paper. JEL Classifications: M42; M41; L81; G14.

papers.title: Scorecard Integration and Cross-Functional Coordination: Joint Effects on Managerial Commitment to ESG Goals
Corporate Culture and Cost Stickiness

The Endurance of Government Connections after the Anti-corruption Campaign in China
How Generative AI Reshapes Analysts’ Information Intermediation: Evidence From China
papers.abstract: This paper examines the relationship between generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) adoption propensity in analyst reports and stock price informativeness. Using Chinese A‐share listed firms from 2023 to 2024, we document that greater GenAI adoption propensity in analyst reports is associated with lower stock price informativeness, reflected in a weaker relation between current stock valuations and future firm profitability. This relationship remains robust across alternative specifications and empirical approaches addressing potential endogeneity concerns. The negative association is more pronounced among non‐state‐owned firms, firms without cross‐listings, during analysts’ busy periods, and for firms receiving greater analyst attention. At the report level, higher GenAI adoption propensity is associated with more cautious language, reflected in abnormal negative tone and greater linguistic hedging, and with greater textual convergence across reports covering the same firm. We also find weaker investment–price sensitivity among firms with higher GenAI adoption propensity, consistent with a reduced informational role of stock prices in corporate investment decisions. Overall, our findings suggest that greater GenAI adoption propensity does not necessarily coincide with more informative stock prices, highlighting potential trade‐offs in analysts' information intermediation.

papers.title: Managerial Ability and Employee Workplace Health and Safety
papers.abstract: This study investigates the relationship between managerial ability to efficiently convert capital into revenue (which we refer to as “managerial ability”) and employee workplace health and safety violations. We document a positive association between managerial ability and employee workplace health and safety violations. This relation is more pronounced in firm environments with weaker labor unionization, and becomes weaker in more innovative firm environments, when executive compensation includes stronger employee workplace health and safety incentives and when CEOs have longer horizons. Collectively, these findings suggest that while higher managerial ability is associated with greater employee workplace health and safety violations, firm environments that emphasize stakeholder protections and longer‐term managerial horizons attenuate this relation. Finally, while employee workplace health and safety violations do not significantly affect short‐ to medium‐term financial performance, they appear to harm long‐term financial performance in firms led by high‐ability managers.

papers.title: Credit Tightening and Earnings Quality
papers.abstract: We investigate the effect of credit tightening on firms’ earnings quality (EQ). During periods of credit tightening, agency conflicts between lenders and borrowers intensify, prompting firms to adjust their EQ to compete for scarce credit resources. Leveraging a unique setting in China, where credit tightening is induced by the crowding‐out effect of local government debt and varies across cities, we find that firms improve EQ in response to credit tightening. The effect is less pronounced for state‐owned enterprises (SOEs) and more pronounced for firms with greater financial constraints and higher growth opportunities. Moreover, we find evidence that firms with improved EQ secure more debt financing and enjoy a lower cost of debt. Our evidence highlights credit tightening as a crucial macroeconomic determinant of firms’ EQ.

papers.title: Forecast Horizon and Peer‐Disclosure Effects: Quarterly Versus Annual Management Forecasts
papers.abstract: Managers often look to industry peers when deciding whether to issue earnings guidance, but peer‐communication effects can differ across forecast horizons. We examine how the association between peer disclosure and a firm's guidance decision varies for quarterly versus annual management forecasts. Using US management forecast data from 2005 to 2024, we estimate dynamic linear probability models in which a firm's disclosure decision depends on the proportion of industry peers issuing guidance for the same time horizon in the prior period. The evidence indicates a clear horizon split—where a higher proportion of peers issuing guidance in the previous period is associated with a higher likelihood that the focal firm will issue quarterly guidance and a lower likelihood that it will issue annual guidance. Additional analyses indicate that these horizon‐specific associations vary in uncertainty‐related settings, consistent with peer disclosure strengthening short‐horizon disclosure pressure while enabling greater substitution with longer horizons.

papers.title: Ancestor's Legacy? The Effect of Folklore on Corporate Innovation
papers.abstract: This paper investigates how ancestral narratives shape contemporary corporate innovation. Drawing on pre‐industrial folklore from 20 countries, we exploit within‐country variation in local cultural motifs to examine their impact on firm innovation. We focus on two types of motifs: narratives depicting heroes’ successful challenges relative to challenge‐losing ones and narratives containing supernatural entities. We show that firms located in societies whose local folklore prevalently features heroes overcoming challenges exhibit greater R&D investment and higher patent‐based innovation efficiency, with directionally similar but statistically insignificant evidence for citation‐based efficiency. In contrast, firms in societies where folklore emphasizes supernatural entities display lower R&D investment and lower innovation efficiency. Cross‐sectional analyses indicate that these effects are moderated by regional economic openness and national patent protection and are more pronounced in highly innovative industries and among firms with higher levels of corporate transparency. Our findings are robust after controlling for regional factors or alleviating large country sample bias. The relationship between folklore and R&D investment remains directionally consistent, albeit with lower statistical significance, after instrumenting the folklore measure with historical immigration patterns to the United States. We further show that the net prevalence of challenge‐encouraging motifs is associated with more radical innovation strategies and greater corporate risk‐taking, while supernatural motifs exhibit the opposite pattern. Overall, our findings support the view that folklore persists across generations and meaningfully influences firms’ contemporary economic decisions and outcomes.

papers.title: Contextualization of Numbers in Earnings Conference Calls
papers.abstract: Prior research generally finds that using numbers in financial disclosure is beneficial. However, numbers can also be strategically proffered due to their perceived precision and informativeness. We find the use of undercontextualized numbers in earnings conference calls is associated with short‐term benefits but negative longer‐term consequences. Specifically, undercontextualization is associated with a short‐term positive market return, positive analyst forecast revisions, and a more positive tone in analysts’ questions. Furthermore, we find undercontextualization is associated with a longer‐term negative market return, a decrease in year‐over‐year earnings, and a higher incidence of restatements. In additional analyses, we find evidence consistent with the intentional use of undercontextualization, as it is associated with conference call casting, insider trading, and internal information quality. Given the uniqueness of our measure, we provide evidence of its validity by documenting its association with analyst scrutiny and other proxies for strategic call behavior. Finally, we examine a mechanism underlying our results and find evidence that undercontextualized numbers have a greater influence on retail investors.

papers.title: Management control across complexity and dynamism: A synthesis of contingency-based research
Does mandatory accounting disclosure of derivatives and hedging activities affect the cost of debt? Evidence from SFAS 161
Standard setters’ use of qualitative characteristics in fair value standards: a Derridean analysis
Correction to “Reporting Connectivity, Audit Quality, and Audit Fees”
Does Corporate Accountability Towards Biodiversity Loss and Species Extinction Protection Account for Audit Efforts: New Insights from External Auditing
papers.abstract: This study investigates whether and how corporate biodiversity disclosure affects external audit efforts. Using a deep‐learning‐expanded text analysis of corporate social responsibility reports for heavily polluting Chinese companies from 2009 to 2021, this paper examines the relation between biodiversity disclosure and audit efforts. The empirical evidence reveals that firms with more extensive biodiversity disclosure exhibit significantly greater external audit efforts. The results remain robust to a series of endogeneity checks, including two‐stage least squares estimation and a combined propensity score matching and difference‐in‐differences analysis. Further analyses show that this positive relation is more pronounced for non‐state‐owned enterprises and firms located in eastern China. Mechanism tests reveal that biodiversity disclosure by heavy polluters triggers a ‘horn effect’, which elevates auditors' perceptions of composite audit risk, thereby driving greater audit effort. Interestingly, while biodiversity disclosures increase audit duration, they do not translate into higher audit fees. Collectively, the findings demonstrate that corporate biodiversity accountability increases audit risk and effort, highlighting the economic consequences of sustainability reporting within the auditing context.

papers.title: Does the Facial Trustworthiness of Hosting Staff Lead to Forecast Bias? Evidence from Analysts’ Site Visits
papers.abstract: We use unique data about corporate site visits in China to examine whether face‐to‐face interactions introduce bias in analyst forecasts. We find that analysts tend to issue more optimistic forecasts when accompanied by hosting staff with high facial trustworthiness, indicating a cognitive bias. This effect is amplified when firms convey more positive information during visits, but is attenuated for firms with high disclosure quality, for experienced and star analysts, for analysts with science, technology, engineering, and mathematics backgrounds, and for analysts visiting industry peers concurrently. Furthermore, the bias is stronger for sole‐visiting analysts but diminishes over time as additional information becomes available or with repeated interactions. Additional analyses show that forecast accuracy also declines, but the effect of facial trustworthiness does not extend to analysts’ stock recommendations or market reactions. Overall, our findings highlight that even sophisticated analysts are susceptible to cognitive bias in face‐to‐face interactions, while alternative information sources, professional experience, and repeated engagement help mitigate such bias.

papers.title: 25 years of the IASB: have the reporting problems been solved?
Domain Knowledge and Human-AI Collaboration: Extracting Accounting Information from Contracts
papers.abstract: SYNOPSIS Contracts govern how firms invest, borrow, and recognize revenue, but their length, technical terms, and nested cross-references make large-sample extraction slow and error-prone. We examine whether generative AI (GenAI) can ease this task and what role accountants’ expertise plays. Framing the division of labor through Becker and Murphy (1992) specialization theory, we develop an iterative, human-in-the-loop prompt engineering workflow in which the model interprets contractual terms and a human verifier corrects its output. Nine variants across debt, lease, and sales contracts vary the presence of a human verification loop and the verifier’s accounting expertise. Accuracy rises with both expertise depth and verification intensity, and the two are complementary. A nonaccountant loop drops accuracy below the no-loop baseline, whereas an accountant reaches higher accuracy at lower cost and catches model failures. For firms and researchers staffing contract analysis, deep human domain knowledge is the scarce input, not only GenAI access. Data Availability: The contracts analyzed in this study are publicly available from SEC EDGAR. The prompts used in each workflow are reproduced in the Online Appendix. JEL Classifications: M41; C81; O33; J24; G32; K12.

papers.title: Trading Patterns Before Unscheduled Corporate Announcements
papers.abstract: SYNOPSIS Using comprehensive trade-level data from India’s National Stock Exchange, covering 1,491 unscheduled corporate announcements between 2011 and 2015, we identify which categories of traders position themselves profitably in the days before public disclosure. Retail traders, and to a lesser extent proprietary manual traders, accumulate positions in the direction of the impending announcement; institutional and algorithmic traders do not. The advantage is concentrated in good news events (consistent with short-sale constraints) and in smaller stocks and is absent before scheduled earnings announcements or randomized placebo events. The pattern is consistent with insider-origin information diffusing through informal networks—broker chatter, messaging app groups, and social media—into a noisy signal that the least constrained traders can act upon but compliance-bound institutions cannot. The findings have implications for the design of pre-announcement disclosure rules and the monitoring of informal communication channels. Data Availability: The NSE trade-level data were obtained from the National Stock Exchange of India for academic research and are subject to the Exchange’s data-sharing restrictions. Announcement and firm-level data are available from the sources cited in the text. JEL Classifications: G14; G15; G18.

papers.title: Temporal Variations in R&D Excess Returns
papers.abstract: SYNOPSIS We examine the time-series behavior of R&D excess returns among U.S. firms over five decades. Controlling for well known risk factors, we find that these returns exist only during the two decades 1970–1979 and 1990–1999. Further analysis suggests that R&D excess returns are consistently significant only from 1992 to 2002 and receive greater support from firm-specific risk explanations than from mispricing explanations. We find that, in addition to exhibiting structural breaks, the temporal variations in R&D excess returns are associated with overall market sentiment, macroeconomic uncertainty, and business R&D spending during the lead-up to and bursting of the 1990s dotcom technology bubble. Further tests show that the disappearance of R&D excess returns post-2002 is associated with reduced arbitrage risk stemming from lower idiosyncratic risk and with the declining presence of younger firms post-2000. Our findings provide new insights into the dynamic and complex nature of R&D excess returns. Data Availability: The data used in this study are available from the Bureau of Economic Analysis, Compustat, CRSP, I/B/E/S, NCSES, and SDC Platinum. JEL Classifications: G14; M41.

papers.title: Comprehensive Review of IFRS Research: A Machine-Assisted Human Approach
papers.abstract: SYNOPSIS Using a machine-assisted human approach, we provide a comprehensive review of 1,041 IFRS articles published in top-tier journals (ABS 4*, 4, and 3) between 1984 and 2025. We combine latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA), a probabilistic topic-modeling technique, with human validation and interpretation to map the thematic structure and development of IFRS research. We identify ten major IFRS research topics and examine the studies that have shaped these research streams and the methodological approaches underlying their development. Citation patterns indicate that research on the topics Economic and financial consequences of IFRS adoption and Convergence and harmonization-related issues in IFRS has attracted particularly strong scholarly attention. Moreover, we document publication trends over the years across several dimensions and identify influential authors and journals in each area. Finally, we assess the usefulness of generative large language models for mapping the IFRS literature, emphasizing both their analytical promise and their methodological limitations. Data Availability: Data used in this paper are from publicly available sources. JEL Classifications: M41; C88; G38.

papers.title: Sources of Differences in Cryptocurrency Tax Software
papers.abstract: SYNOPSIS Cryptocurrency taxation is an increasingly important topic of interest for policymakers, regulators, and taxpayers. Tax compliance efforts related to cryptocurrency have led to mandatory reporting for all individual taxpayers, have been the subject of multiple rounds of guidance by the Internal Revenue Service, and have spawned a billion-dollar industry of cryptocurrency experts who offer taxpayers solutions to the complex reporting requirements. I examine whether these solutions produce consistent and reliable outputs. Using the same set of transactions across multiple providers, I document evidence of significant variation in the calculation of taxable income. These discrepancies should be of particular concern as cryptocurrency exchanges, tax preparers, and the IRS prepare for and assess third-party reporting of cryptocurrency transactions. JEL Classifications: H20; K34; M49.

papers.title: Risk Governance: A Way to Promote Ethical Business in Organizations
papers.abstract: SYNOPSIS Regulators seek to make organizations more ethical by imposing requirements for risk governance. However, the academic and practitioner literature questions whether regulators’ objective has been met. In this paper, based on a field study in the financial services industry, we describe innovative practices in risk governance at three companies that seem to have succeeded in mitigating some of their ethical issues. We thereby contribute to the practice of risk governance and show that risk governance can indeed foster ethics. Data Availability: Data consists of our confidential notes from the field visits. JEL Classifications: M40; K20; G32.

papers.title: The Accounting Pipeline Challenge: Insights from Accounting Firm Leaders
papers.abstract: SYNOPSIS We interview 14 accounting firm leaders to understand the accounting pipeline challenge from the profession’s perspective. The interviews confirm some prior findings about the pipeline and offer new insights in four areas. First, interviewees do not view the shortage uniformly, including mixed views on the quality of entrants and interviewees viewing the shortage as more severe for the profession than for their firm. Second, interviewees indicate that the shortage is associated with many consequences within firms (e.g., increased workload and stress). Third, interviewees suggest that traditional responses to the shortage, such as higher compensation and enhanced retention strategies, may be reaching their limit. Finally, interviewees suggest that the profession is seeking new solutions to the shortage, including managing artificial intelligence (AI) versus human factors. We also find notable differences between major market/Big 4 firms and other firms. We discuss implications and future research directions in this rapidly changing environment.

papers.title: ESG in Executive Pay: Prevalence, Design, Role Alignment, and Gaps
papers.abstract: SYNOPSIS Using named executive officer (NEO)-level data for Russell 3000 firms from 2021 to 2024, we describe how firms incorporate environmental, social, and governance (ESG) metrics into executive compensation. ESG pay design varies across industries and executive functions in ways broadly consistent with incentive compatibility. However, ESG metrics remain concentrated in short-term incentive plans and are rarely embedded in equity awards. Explicit weights are much more common than modifiers, limiting the extent to which ESG performance affects total pay. In emission-intensive industries, firms quantify goals more often than reported outcomes, creating asymmetry between ex ante expectation and ex post performance. Overall, ESG-linked pay exhibits substantial role alignment, but important design gaps remain. The evidence provides benchmarks for compensation committees designing ESG pay, investors, and stakeholders evaluating pay practices, regulators, and researchers evaluating ESG-linked compensation. Data Availability: Data are commercially available from the sources cited in the text. JEL Classifications: M40; M41.

papers.title: Discretionary Impairments of Finite and Indefinite Intangible Assets
papers.abstract: SYNOPSIS Motivated by the debate on how post-acquisition accounting should treat different types of intangibles, particularly the choice between amortization and impairment versus impairment-only approaches, we use hand-collected data on acquired intangible assets and their impairments to examine the determinants of impairments of finite and indefinite intangible assets and goodwill. Impairments of indefinite-lived intangibles and goodwill are more strongly associated with reporting-related conditions than are impairments of finite-lived intangibles, which also exhibit modest associations with economic impairment indicators. Moreover, internal governance mechanisms moderate the relation between impairment pressure and recognized impairments for indefinite-lived intangibles and goodwill, but much less so for finite-lived intangibles, consistent with greater scope for discretion under the impairment-only regime. Our results are relevant for policymakers considering proposals to subsume intangible assets into goodwill and modify impairment test procedures. Data Availability: Data are available from the public sources cited in the text.

papers.title: How Shared Values between Assurance Providers and Clients Can Impair Professional Skepticism: A Quasi-Experiment
papers.abstract: We conduct a quasi-experiment to test whether assurance providers whose personal values align with those of a client exhibit weaker skeptical judgments and actions than those without such alignment. Drawing on value congruence theory, we predict and find that shared values indirectly reduce skeptical action through increased client trust and reduced skeptical judgment. We further show that moral identity (an individual trait) functions as a self-regulatory consistency mechanism that strengthens the link between skeptical judgment and skeptical action, such that those higher on moral identity are more likely to act on their skeptical judgments, amplifying this indirect effect. Shared values are operationalized using a for-profit client’s charitable initiative. As social initiatives and other forms of corporate value signaling become more common, our findings highlight a timely paradox: value congruence can foster trust that enhances relationships—but at a potential cost to professional skepticism. Data Availability: Data are available from the authors upon request.

papers.title: Mapping urban poverty: The unfolding of competing accounts through accounting visualizations
“Blamestorming” in Central‐Local Government Relations? A Discourse Analysis of Blame amid English Local Government Failure
papers.abstract: This article explores how blame manifests in central‐local government relations in conditions of failure. The financial challenges facing English local government have reached a tipping point in recent years, illustrated by sharp increases in central government intervention, local government “bankruptcy”, and requests for “exceptional financial support”. We report on the assembly of a new, comprehensive dataset of central‐local intervention in fiscal distress between 2020 and 2026, comprising 51 Best Value Notices, Inspections, External Assurance Reviews (EAR), and Section 114 Notices. We employ Hood's blame framework in a discourse analysis of these documents, illuminating the presentational, agency, and policy strategies used to attribute blame. We find these four document types, rather than a cohesive architecture for intervention, operate as distinct discursive regimes which locate blame. The article illustrates a current system which is characterized by traditions of central control and assurance, with the current statutory and fiscal intervention approaches creating further challenges to sectoral improvement, fiscal sustainability, and locally led devolution. The article illustrates the complex and incohesive nature of current statutory and fiscal intervention instruments and cautions that the preoccupation with blame may prove counterproductive to sectoral improvement and fiscal sustainability.

papers.title: The Impact of Board Gender Diversity on Audit Pricing: The Case of Greek Local Governments
papers.abstract: We study the effect of gender diversity on public‐sector auditing by analyzing the impact of female representation on audit pricing in Greek local government (LG) boards. Adopting a theoretically pluralistic approach, we find that increased female representation lowers the price of audits. This is primarily due to a perceived reduction in audit risk. This negative effect is more pronounced when the power of political opposition is weak, and the number of females on the board reaches a critical mass of 30%. Our results are robust to model specifications and endogeneity. We conclude that audit pricing, as an agency cost, is reduced because female LG representation decreases the need to bear the costs of monitoring agents.

papers.title: Recent Reforms of Intergovernmental Grants for Local Governments in Germany: Consequences for Accountability and Oversight
papers.abstract: Germany's intergovernmental grant system faces mounting complexity and administrative burden. Recent reforms seek to reduce bureaucracy through lump‐sum funding, decentralized audits, and outcome‐focused approaches. Drawing on Second Generation Fiscal Federalism Theory and program implementation research, this article analyzes three reform cases: climate protection grants, audit decentralization in North Rhine‐Westphalia, and social block grants in Saxony. We identify a critical trade‐off: Simplification efforts enhance procedural efficiency but may weaken oversight and accountability. The findings reveal that reform design determines whether accountability gaps emerge. We conclude that formular‐based allocation, indicator‐based evaluation, or decentralized audit capacity can balance flexibility with accountability in a less bureaucratic fiscal environment.
