papers.title: A Direct Method to Imply Activity-Level Required Returns: Evidence From Firms With Bifurcated Business Models
papers.abstract: Implied cost of capital (ICC) models have been limited to the firm level because activity-level market values are unobservable. We develop a novel method for firms with two main activities that resolves this challenge by using share price pairs to solve simultaneous accounting-based valuation equations for each activity. We empirically validate the method using a specific dataset of international banks with bifurcated business models, demonstrating that the resulting ICCs have an appropriate dependency structure, are correctly rank-ordered, and are economically rational. While our empirical analysis focuses on this distinct set of firms, use cases illustrate the method’s broad applicability to other multi-activity contexts, such as asset management, divestitures and commercial lending. Our method has the potential to improve accuracy in capital budgeting, managerial performance evaluation, and business valuations.

papers.journal: Journal of Accounting Auditing and Finance
papers.title: Learning While Working: How Do Early Litigation Experiences Affect Managers’ Disclosure?
papers.abstract: We track the employment histories of over 6,000 chief executive officers (CEOs) and study how their past litigation experiences affect voluntary disclosure of management forecasts. We define litigation experience to be any securities class action experienced during a CEO’s early career in non-CEO positions and in other firms. We find that CEOs with litigation experience (“litigation CEOs”) provide more management forecasts. The positive effects are further identified using a matched sample design. We also find that litigation CEOs provide more timely forecasts, are more likely to provide range forecasts, and market reactions to their forecasts are stronger. Collectively, the evidence indicates that early career litigation exposure leads CEOs to improve both the quantity and quality of their voluntary disclosures.

papers.title: Internationalising accounting and finance education under conditional globalisation
papers.abstract: Purpose This paper examines how accounting and finance education acquires international value within a conditionally globalised environment, and how professional recognition relates to universities' epistemic and public-interest legitimacy. Design/methodology/approach The paper develops a conceptual framework through an integrative discussion of accounting and finance education, internationalisation, signalling, legitimacy and professions research. Australian educational arrangements and published research illustrate the institutional relationships. Findings International value depends on interdependent relationships among university legitimacy, professional recognition, regulatory credibility, employer reputation, mobility opportunities and public-interest formation. Their importance varies by audience, discipline and jurisdiction. Professional recognition can amplify educational credibility when it complements knowledge formation; its dominance can weaken legitimacy when it displaces critical inquiry. Four propositions specify these relationships and their boundaries. Originality/value The paper conceptualises international accounting and finance education as reputational infrastructure. It connects conditional cross-border value with the productive tension between professional legibility and universities' responsibilities as custodians, critics and producers of knowledge, while distinguishing the disciplines' recognition pathways.

papers.title: Climate change policy and climate risk disclosure: evidence from machine learning and textual analysis
papers.abstract: Purpose This study examines how National Climate Change Policy (NCCP) influences firm-level climate risk disclosure (CRD). The study also investigates whether the policy affects transition- and physical-risk disclosure differently, and how analyst coverage, political connections and CSR intensity shape this relationship. Design/methodology/approach The study uses firm-year data for companies listed on the Pakistan Stock Exchange from 2007 to 2022. CRD is measured using a hybrid computational linguistics framework that combines Word2Vec embeddings, semantic expansion and multi-stage expert validation to construct separate disclosure indices for transition and physical risk. The empirical analysis employs an exposure-based difference-in-differences design. Findings The results show that NCCP affects climate disclosure selectively rather than uniformly. The policy significantly increases physical-risk disclosure, whereas transition-risk disclosure declines in the baseline specification. Dynamic estimates support parallel trends and indicate that the effects emerge gradually. Further analysis shows that policy-relevant political connections are associated with stronger disclosure responses, while higher CSR intensity mitigates the decline in transition-risk disclosure and amplifies the increase in physical-risk disclosure. Analyst coverage provides suggestive evidence of an information-intermediary channel. Practical implications The findings suggest that climate policy alone may not be sufficient to ensure broad-based transparency in a weak-enforcement environment. Stricter mandatory rules, better institutional coordination and external monitoring may improve corporate climate transparency. Originality/value This study provides evidence from a climate-vulnerable emerging economy and introduces a validated text-based CRD measure that distinguishes transition-risk from physical-risk disclosure and shows that policy effects depend on political access, external monitoring and strategic capacity.

papers.title: Data-driven capability and corporate cost stickiness: evidence from information processing, expectation revision, and governance transparency
papers.abstract: Purpose Existing literature explains cost stickiness primarily through adjustment costs, managerial optimism, and agency conflicts, but overlooks the role of data-driven capability at the micro-foundational level. This study aims to investigate how a firm's data-driven capability reshapes asymmetric cost behaviour and to uncover its underlying micro-mechanisms. Design/methodology/approach Using a sample of Chinese A-share listed firms from 2013 to 2024, this study constructs a firm-level measure of data-driven capability via textual analysis. We employ empirical regressions to examine its effect on cost stickiness, supported by sensitivity checks and endogeneity corrections. We further conduct mechanism and heterogeneity tests, and examine the effect on administrative expense stickiness. Findings Data-driven capability is significantly associated with lower cost stickiness, a result robust to endogeneity corrections. Mechanism analyses provide suggestive evidence consistent with three channels: information processing, expectation formation, and governance transparency. The association is more pronounced in firms with higher business complexity and severe agency conflicts, and is also significantly associated with lower administrative expense stickiness. These findings uncover the micro-mechanisms through which data-driven capability influences cost adjustment behaviour. Originality/value This study is original in extending the cost stickiness literature by introducing data-driven capability as a novel micro-foundational determinant, moving beyond traditional cost and agency perspectives. By employing textual analysis to construct a firm-level measure, it provides a new methodological approach. The value of this research lies in uncovering the specific micro-mechanisms driving asymmetric cost behaviour and offering practical implications for digital-era cost management, helping managers understand how data resources optimise resource allocation during demand contractions.

papers.title: From exposure to imprint: CEO formative experiences and the architecture of accounting and financial decisions
papers.abstract: Purpose This review explains how chief executive officers' formative experiences become organizationally consequential and why apparently similar exposures are associated with different accounting, financing, risk and stakeholder decisions. Design/methodology/approach Following the Search-Appraisal-Analysis-Synthesis (SAAS) workflow, the study maps 105 Scopus-indexed journal articles published between 2011 and 2026 using Biblioshiny and VOSviewer and conducts a structured content synthesis of 102 studies whose focal construct is an executive formative experience. Findings The literature converges around upper-echelons and imprinting perspectives but does not support a uniform “adversity produces conservatism” account. The synthesis distinguishes four adversity-related imprint families – threat vigilance and loss avoidance; uncertainty habituation, resilience or self-efficacy; scarcity orientation; and prosocial reorientation – while treating institutional socialization as conceptually distinct. Persistent imprints become observable only when later situations activate them and when executive discretion permits expression. Accounting and financing architecture provides particularly discriminating tests of these mechanisms. Originality/value The review moves beyond exposure–outcome associations by separating exposure formation, imprint content, activation, expression and observed decision bundles. It recentres accounting and corporate finance in the chief executive officer formative-experience literature and develops an auditable mechanism-based research agenda.

papers.title: What non-financial disclosure research can (and cannot) learn from financial disclosure research about impression management – a structured literature review
papers.abstract: Purpose This paper reviews the literature on impression management (IM) in corporate disclosures and systematically compares research on financial disclosures (FD) and non-financial disclosures (NFD), particularly sustainability reporting. Given the maturity of IM research in FD and the recent acceleration of IM research in NFD driven by societal and regulatory pressures, the study aims to identify commonalities, differences, and research gaps between both streams, and to assess how insights from FD research can inform future IM research in NFD. Design/methodology/approach We conduct a structured review of 83 archival studies published since 2000 in leading accounting and sustainability journals. The review compares FD and NFD studies along key dimensions, including motivators of IM, disclosure instruments, sample characteristics, and econometric approaches, thereby enabling a systematic assessment of methodological and conceptual differences between the two research streams. Findings The review yields four main findings. First, theoretical frameworks in NFD research remain largely disconnected from capital-market considerations that anchor FD research. Second, NFD research focuses predominantly on sustainability performance as a motivator of IM, leaving other motivators – such as CSR contracting, investor sustainability preferences, and political influence – largely unexplored. Third, prior studies emphasize textual IM instruments, while visual and structural elements central to sustainability reporting remain underexamined. Fourth, NFD studies typically rely on smaller samples and less rigorous econometric designs than FD research, limiting robustness and replicability. Originality/value This study systematically compares archival IM research across FD and NFD. By synthesizing insights from the mature FD literature, it develops a research agenda that broadens the scope of IM motivators, advances the measurement of visual and structural disclosure practices, and strengthens methodological rigor in future NFD research.

papers.title: Overconfident chief executive officers in capital structure decision-making – a systematic literature review
papers.abstract: Purpose This systematic literature review (SLR) synthesises and integrates the growing body of research on CEO overconfidence and corporate capital structure decisions, with particular attention to how alternative measures of overconfidence may contribute to divergent findings. Design/methodology/approach This review systematically searched EconLit, Scopus, Web of Science, Business Source Ultimate and Google Scholar using terms covering CEO overconfidence and capital structure. After screening and eligibility assessment, we reviewed 53 studies and coded them by overconfidence proxy, research method, treatment of endogeneity, identification strategy and findings. Findings The review finds substantial heterogeneity in the operationalisation of CEO overconfidence. These measures are not conceptually equivalent and differ in construct validity and susceptibility to endogeneity and measurement error. The apparent inconsistency in findings should be interpreted cautiously: differences may reflect measurement and identification choices as well as institutional and firm-level context. Originality/value This review clarifies how measurement heterogeneity and differences in empirical identification shape conclusions about CEO overconfidence and capital structure. It also identifies priorities for future research, including construct triangulation, stronger causal designs and transparent reporting of alternative measures.

papers.title: The irrelevant responses and stock liquidity: dual validation evidence from the Chinese stock market using machine learning and large language models
papers.abstract: Purpose As China’s capital market advances toward higher-quality development, the quality of corporate information disclosure and the transparency of managerial communication have become central concerns for investors and regulators. This study examines the relationship between managerial irrelevant responses during site visits and stock liquidity, and further investigates the underlying mechanisms through which such responses affect market liquidity. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on Q&A records from site visits to A-share listed companies in China, this study constructs a quantitative measure of managerial irrelevant responses using machine learning techniques. In addition, online scoring based on a large language model (GPT-4) is introduced as a complementary indicator. Using regression analyses, we estimate the impact of irrelevant responses on stock liquidity and conduct mechanism and subgroup analyses to ensure robustness. Findings We find that managerial irrelevant responses are significantly negatively associated with stock liquidity. Mechanism analyses suggest that increased investor attention to financial issues reflects heightened uncertainty about firms’ future prospects, thereby exacerbating illiquidity. Furthermore, evasive or ambiguous managerial communication reduces analyst coverage, deteriorates the external information environment and further suppresses stock liquidity. Subgroup analyses reveal that this negative effect is more pronounced among firms without a price limit mechanism, firms with lower institutional ownership and firms receiving limited media attention. Originality/value This study contributes to the literature at the intersection of information disclosure and market microstructure by introducing a novel, text-based measure of managerial communication quality. The findings provide evidence on the real market consequences of evasive disclosure behavior and offer important policy implications for improving regulatory oversight and managerial communication practices in capital markets.

papers.title: CEO overconfidence and the linguistic representation of corporate culture in 10-K filings: evidence from upper echelons theory
papers.abstract: Purpose This study examines whether chief executive officer (CEO) overconfidence is associated with the linguistic representation of corporate culture in mandatory 10-K filings. Drawing on upper echelons theory, we argue that executives' psychological traits surface not only in strategic and financial outcomes but in the language through which corporate culture is communicated to external stakeholders, across the dimensions of control, collaboration, competition, and creation. Design/methodology/approach Using 27,742 firm-year observations from 2000 to 2022 drawn from Compustat, ExecuComp, and BoardEx, we measure CEO overconfidence through established option-exercise, stockholding, and investment proxies, and culture through textual analysis of 10-K filings. We estimate ordinary least squares models with year and industry fixed effects and assess robustness using firm fixed-effects models, lagged specifications, propensity score matching, entropy balancing, Heckman selection models, and instrumental variables. Findings CEO overconfidence is negatively associated with all four dimensions of culture-related language, with particularly pronounced associations for collective and procedural themes. The findings are robust across alternative specifications and identification strategies. The association is attenuated under female CEOs and more gender-diverse boards, concentrated in the discretionary Management Discussion and Analysis section, and accompanied by more optimistic and self-referential language, consistent with a managerial communication channel. Culture-related language is also associated with greater audit effort and market uncertainty and lower future performance. Supplementary pathway analysis reveals significant indirect associations for two overconfidence measures, linking the documented disclosure channel to economically relevant firm outcomes. Originality/value We extend upper echelons theory to the linguistic domain of regulated disclosure, showing that culture-specific language carries traces of managerial cognition even in collectively produced filings. By distinguishing control, collaboration, competition, and creation, the study also provides a practical framework through which auditors, boards, and reporting professionals can interpret culture-related language as a supplementary signal of managerial orientation, governance tone, and narrative-reporting risk.

papers.title: Credibility displacement in algorithmic financial reporting: a critical review of AI, disclosure credibility and capital-market consequences
papers.abstract: Purpose This review examines how financial-reporting credibility is shaped when algorithmic systems enter the reporting chain. It asks where credibility is produced, tested and understood when artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning, large language models, eXtensible Business Reporting Language (XBRL) analytics and related tools affect reporting information. Design/methodology/approach The paper combines a search and screening procedure informed by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) with a concept-centric synthesis. The evidence base comprises a 226-paper curated core and a 144-paper close-synthesis subset. Sensitivity analyses re-examine the 39-record outlet boundary and the close-synthesis threshold. Findings The evidence remains dispersed across research on textual disclosure and natural language processing (NLP), audit analytics and assurance, structured reporting using XBRL, market interpretation, accounting information systems (AIS) implementation and AI governance. Across these streams, algorithms can improve reporting processes but may also alter the grounds on which reporting assertions are accepted. We describe the latter possibility as credibility displacement: model-related output, provenance or validation partly substitutes for scrutiny of the underlying assertion or for identifiable professional and institutional safeguards. Originality/value The review defines algorithmic financial reporting as a reporting-chain phenomenon rather than a general label for technology adoption. It distinguishes four sites: preparation, assurance, machine-readable presentation and algorithmic interpretation. Governance operates across these sites as a cross-cutting condition, making the proposed displacement mechanism more focused and empirically testable.

papers.title: Modern slavery governance, digital transformation and financial distress risk: evidence from legally grounded text-based accounting measures
papers.abstract: Purpose This paper aims to develop and validate a legally grounded accounting measurement framework for modern-slavery governance and examines whether the resulting governance measures are associated with firms' financial distress risk. Existing research predominantly relies on ESG ratings, disclosure proxies, or qualitative assessments that do not clearly distinguish externally specified governance obligations from firms' disclosed governance architecture. We address this measurement gap by translating mandatory modern-slavery governance requirements into reproducible firm-level accounting measures and evaluating their informational relevance for accounting-based risk assessment. Design/methodology/approach This research adopts a two-corpus measurement framework. The first corpus comprises mandatory modern-slavery legislation and internationally recognised institutional frameworks issued between 1930 and 2024, including the Tariff Act (1930), California Transparency in Supply Chains Act, UK Modern Slavery Act, French Duty of Vigilance Law, Australian Modern Slavery Act, German Supply Chain Due Diligence Act, Norwegian Transparency Act, the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD), the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD), and complementary institutional frameworks including the ILO, OECD, PRI, and the United Nations Guiding Principles. Rather than serving as institutional background, these sources are used to define the governance construct by identifying legally codified organisational obligations and harmonising them into a unified governance ontology representing implementation-oriented governance mechanisms.The second corpus comprises more than 5,000 annual reports of S&P 500 firms covering the period 2010–2022. Artificial intelligence (AI), natural language processing (NLP), and supervised machine-learning techniques operationalise the predefined governance ontology to identify disclosed evidence of implementation-oriented governance mechanisms within corporate reports, thereby generating firm-year Modern Slavery Index (MSI) measures. A complementary Digital Transformation Index (DTI) captures disclosed digital capability. The empirical design combines firm and year fixed-effects estimation with 2SLS endogeneity-sensitivity analysis and additional tests addressing disclosure intensity and boilerplate reporting, institutional validity, digital-capability interactions, competing explanations and potential mechanisms. Findings The findings show that firms disclosing stronger implementation-oriented modern-slavery governance mechanisms exhibit lower financial distress risk, although the strength of this association varies across the underlying institutional architectures. Among the four governance measures, the California-based MSI2 provides the strongest evidence, indicating that disclosed governance mechanisms centred on supplier verification, monitoring, accountability, and supply-chain oversight are associated with lower financial distress risk. Digital transformation, by contrast, does not independently reduce financial distress risk and is associated with lower Altman Z-scores in several specifications, a pattern consistent with – but not establishing – the organisational costs and implementation challenges that may accompany technological transformation. Importantly, digital capability also conditions the association between disclosed modern-slavery governance and financial distress risk, with the positive MSI4 × DTI interaction indicating that the financial relevance of governance disclosure varies with firms' digital capabilities under particular institutional arrangements. Overall, the findings indicate that legally grounded measures of disclosed modern-slavery governance contain economically relevant information for financial-distress assessment, while their associations vary across governance architectures and according to firms' digital capabilities. Originality/value This paper makes four contributions to the accounting literature. First, it develops four transparent, legally grounded, and fully reproducible Modern Slavery Indices (MSI1–MSI4), each derived from distinct regulatory and institutional governance frameworks, providing researchers, practitioners, managers, auditors, and policymakers with standardised accounting measures of implementation-oriented modern-slavery governance. Second, it introduces a novel two-corpus measurement framework that explicitly separates construct definition from empirical observation by deriving the governance construct from mandatory legislation and internationally recognised frameworks before operationalising it through AI-enabled textual analysis of corporate reports. Third, it demonstrates how artificial intelligence, natural language processing, and supervised machine-learning techniques can operationalise externally defined governance obligations into scalable firm-level accounting information while preserving construct validity. Finally, it provides evidence that these legally grounded accounting measures contain decision-useful information for accounting-based risk assessment, advancing research on non-financial accounting measurement, governance architecture, disclosure credibility, internal control systems, and corporate resilience under emerging mandatory reporting regimes.

papers.title: Ethics and climate litigation: from case law to knowledge networks
papers.abstract: Purpose This article examines how climate litigation has evolved from a policy instrument into a legal mechanism for enforcing ethical obligations, positioning climate change as an ethical issue and identifying human rights as a litigation outcome. Design/methodology/approach Adopting the design of an integrative literature review, the study combines bibliometric mapping of Web of Science citation data, processed using Bibliometrix and Biblioshiny, with conceptual and doctrinal analysis of key climate litigation case law. Findings Climate change litigation is maturing not only in scope but in ethical grounding, with human rights emerging as a strategic outcome courts increasingly pursue. Using bibliometric analysis, this article maps the intersection of climate litigation and ethics, identifying five research areas: greenhouse gases as pollutants, duty of care, climate science, global climate policy and intercountry equity. Cross-jurisdictional themes show that judicial decisions do more than resolve individual disputes – they shape, legitimize and accelerate transnational governance responses to climate change, positioning courts as meaningful actors in addressing climate change as an ethical imperative. Social implications This study maps the acceptance of ethics within legal spheres as part of the climate debate. Originality/value The article is among the first to integrate bibliometric mapping with doctrinal and ethical analysis of climate litigation, and proposes a tiered research agenda that addresses the interplay between government objectives and the interests of litigants.

papers.title: The SEC's Proposed Rule on Semiannual Reporting: Policy Analysis and Research Agenda
papers.abstract: This commentary has two objectives. First, we summarize a July 2026 comment letter submitted to the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) by members of the Financial Reporting Policy Committee of the Financial Accounting and Reporting Section of the American Accounting Association in response to the SEC’s proposal to permit semiannual interim reporting for Securities Exchange Act reporting companies. Drawing on relevant academic research, we conclude that the proposal’s potential benefits for public market participation, compliance costs, managerial short-termism, and proprietary costs are uncertain and likely modest, whereas the potential costs to consistency, comparability, timeliness, and the public information environment are more substantial and better supported by existing evidence. Second, building on gaps in the existing evidence, we identify promising avenues for future research that could advance the debate over interim reporting frequency and inform future regulatory decisions. JEL Classifications: M40; M41; M48.

papers.title: A Framework for Mitigating the Effects of Large Number Innumeracy in Corporate Disclosures
papers.abstract: As corporate disclosures increasingly report figures in the millions, billions, and trillions, large number innumeracy may systematically distort how investors interpret firm performance. This cognitive limitation arises when individuals compress large magnitudes on the mental number line, overestimating absolute values while underestimating differences between them. We introduce large number innumeracy as a distinct perceptual construct in the accounting literature and synthesize cognitive science and accounting research to explain how it may affect investor interpretation of corporate disclosures and why susceptibility likely varies across investor types. We develop a mitigation framework organized by how directly each mechanism addresses the problem: direct approaches alter how values are represented, contextual supports aid interpretation without changing magnitude representation, and interpretive intermediaries shift processing to outside actors or automated tools. We conclude with a research agenda on prevalence, capital market consequences, and mitigation, with implications for disclosure design, investor protection, and market efficiency. Data Availability: Data are available from the public sources cited in the text. JEL Classifications: M41; G41; D91; D83.

papers.title: Disclosures of Clinical Trials and Analysts’ Target Prices
papers.abstract: Synopsis The research problem This paper examines whether clinical trial disclosures are useful for financial analysts in evaluating biotechs and pharmas. Specifically, we examine the impact of such disclosures on analyst target price revisions and accuracy improvement. Motivation or theoretical reasoning The Food and Drug Administration Amendments Act of 2007, Section 801, requires pharmaceutical companies to disclose clinical trial results on ClinicalTrials.gov, but the National Institutes of Health’s interpretation of the law created a significant exemption from the reporting requirements until 2020. As a result, clinical trials with negative outcomes were often hidden from the public. We examine whether financial analysts nevertheless paid attention to such disclosures and whether this nonfinancial information helped them to better assess the value of biotechs and pharmas. The test hypotheses The first hypothesis states that the intensity of clinical trial disclosure has a positive effect on the magnitude of target price revisions. We expect these revisions to be greater for biotech companies than for pharma. The second hypothesis is that the more intense the disclosures, the higher the probability of setting an accurate target price. Again, we expect a greater improvement for biotechs. Target population The empirical analysis is based on 11,773 target price changes available in I/B/E/S from 2011 to 2017 and 11,407 clinical trial disclosures on the ClinicalTrials.gov website. Adopted methodology We use panel data regression models. Analyses We analyze biotechs and pharmas together and separately, as they exhibit different levels of uncertainty and information asymmetry regarding future cash flows. Their incentives for disclosing the results of clinical trials also differ. Findings The results suggest that clinical trial disclosures lead to larger target price revisions and make it likely that target prices are more accurate. As expected, these disclosures have a greater impact on biotechs.

papers.title: Board Interlocks and Corporate Risk Disclosures
papers.abstract: Synopsis The research problem This study examined how board interlocks influence the content and quality of corporate risk disclosures in U.S. public firms. Although firms are mandated to report material risks in their annual reports, it remains unclear how they identify which risks to disclose and whether shared board members shape this process. The central question of this study is whether directors with multiple board memberships facilitate the transfer of risk information across firms, and whether such transfers enhance or undermine disclosure quality. Motivation Risk disclosure plays a critical role in investor decision-making and regulatory compliance but also poses proprietary and reputational risks. While prior literature emphasizes the role of board structure in disclosure practices, the impact of interlocking directorates—shared directors between firms—remains underexplored in the context of textual risk disclosures. The test hypotheses The first hypothesis tests whether firms disclose a higher number of similar risk factors when they are interlocked through a shared director. The second hypothesis tests whether the quality of a newly disclosed risk factor is associated with the disclosure of a similar risk by a linked firm. Target population This study investigated the Item 1A risk reports of U.S. public firms. Adopted methodology The study employed a stacked regression estimator, which generalizes two-way fixed-effects difference-in-differences (TWFEDID) by allowing for dynamic and heterogeneous treatment effects, OLS regressions, and textual analysis of archival data. Analyses We applied the Top2Vec topic modeling technique to identify and compare the contents of 45,205 Item 1A sections from nonfinancial U.S. public firms between 2006 and 2023. The stacked regression estimator model tested whether firms connected through shared directors disclose more risk factors on the same topics than similar, nonconnected firms. We assessed disclosure quality using specificity, length, and readability metrics. We estimated OLS regressions on risk factor-firm-year observations to evaluate whether the quality of newly disclosed risk factors is affected by prior disclosures from interlocked firms. Findings We found that interlocked firms simultaneously disclose more risk factors with the same topic, particularly when the shared director is an executive director. Further, the shared risk factors between interlocked firms are often less specific, shorter, and harder to read, indicating reduced disclosure quality. Our findings suggest that board interlocks generate imitation rather than insight, producing more boilerplate risk disclosures instead of informative knowledge spillovers.

papers.title: Discussion: Disclosures of Clinical Trials and Analysts’ Target Prices
papers.abstract: Dubois et al. ( 2026 ) studied whether clinical-trial disclosures help financial analysts revise target prices and improve target-price accuracy for biotechnology and pharmaceutical firms. This discussion focuses on how the institutional setting and key features of the empirical design shape the interpretation of the paper’s findings. I argue that the setting is central because the sample period reflects a transitional disclosure regime in which clinical-trial reporting was legally salient but not yet fully enforced. This regime creates meaningful variation in disclosure behavior, but it also raises concerns about selection and timing. I further discuss how the biotech-pharma comparison may obscure heterogeneity in disclosure content, firm characteristics, and disclosure incentives, such that the stronger associations for biotechnology firms may not be driven by information asymmetry alone. I conclude by outlining future research opportunities on mandatory disclosure, disclosure timing, disclosure content, and the real effects of clinical-trial transparency.

Climate Finance Accountability, Transnational Governance and Supreme Audit Institutions
papers.abstract: Using interview evidence from Paris Agreement countries, interpreted through assemblage theory and epistemic communities, we show Supreme Audit Institutions (SAIs) as co‐producers of climate finance accountability. SAIs translate transnational norms of accountability into domestic audit practices through engagement with the International Organisation of Supreme Audit Institutions and its regional affiliates. These agencies serve as boundary‐spanning epistemic communities that build capacity for climate finance audits. Unclear definitions and opaque funding channels limit stand‐alone climate finance audits. Donor‐country SAIs prioritise performance audits tied to national policy while recipient‐country SAIs integrate donor‐funded climate initiatives into national systems.

papers.title: Disclosure as a Signal, Innovation as Validation: Climate Disclosure by China's Heavily Polluting Firms and Green Investor Engagement
papers.abstract: Using a sample of heavily polluting firms listed on China's A‐share market, this study develops an integrated framework linking signal transmission to legitimacy restoration in the context of China's carbon‐peaking and carbon‐neutrality goals and green finance system. Climate risks disclosure of high‐pulluting enterprises (CDHPE) serves both as a compliance baseline and as a costly signal. Mandatory disclosure establishes a general obligation, while voluntary disclosure beyond the minimum requirements, subject to regulatory scrutiny, enforcement and performance review, can serve as a credible and difficult‐to‐imitate signal of transition. The study develops a Chinese‐language CDHPE dictionary using a CBOW word‐embedding model trained on annual reports from A‐share‐listed firms and combines data from multiple sources to identify green investors. The empirical results show that CDHPE significantly increases green investor entry and participation. A one‐standard‐deviation increase in CDHPE raises the probability of entry by 4.47 percentage points (approximately 13.5%) and participation intensity by 5.65%. Reduced information asymmetry, restored corporate credibility and increased environmental investment partially mediate this relationship. The effect is stronger among firms facing greater profit pressure or weaker media oversight, non‐state‐owned firms and firms without ESG certification. Further analysis shows that CDHPE and green investor participation jointly promote high‐quality green innovation. CDHPE's effect on innovation quality, measured by patent citations (4.85%), exceeds its effect on innovation quantity, measured by patent applications (2.95%). This pattern may help counter the quantity‐over‐quality bias in patent incentives. CDHPE also increases green investor shareholdings by 3.93%. Theoretically, the study extends signalling theory beyond a static sender–receiver model to a dynamic process of signal transmission, capital inflow, innovation validation and legitimacy restoration. It also extends dual legitimacy theory by identifying how firm‐level signals contribute to legitimacy restoration. The policy implications support coordinating mandatory disclosure with third‐party carbon verification, enforcement by the Ministry of Ecology and Environment , green‐credit assessments and media oversight. Such coordination can help translate disclosure commitments into credible actions and financing for the low‐carbon transition.

papers.title: Do Boilerplate Green Narratives Affect Responsible Investment Decisions? Evidence From ESG Mutual Funds in China
papers.abstract: This paper employs natural language processing to measure boilerplate in green narratives and examines its effects on responsible investment decisions in China. We find that green narrative boilerplate discourages investment by responsible investors. This may be because boilerplate reduces the effective information available to investors and raises suspicions of poor environmental performance. The negative association is stronger among firms with higher overall information transparency, lower media coverage, and more intense product‐market competition. Boilerplate primarily affects investment selection rather than post‐investment holdings. Our findings offer implications for improving environmental disclosure and the efficiency of responsible investment.

papers.title: Corporate Blockchain Disclosure and Investor Site Visits
papers.abstract: Using a sample of Chinese A‐share listed firms from 2012 to 2021, this study examines how corporate blockchain disclosure affects investor site visits through a staggered difference‐in‐differences design. We find that corporate blockchain disclosure significantly increases investor site visit activity. Disclosing firms are more likely to receive site visits, investors raise more blockchain‐related questions, and managers provide more detailed responses. We further show that investor site visits act as a potential channel through which blockchain disclosure influences long‐term firm value. Cross‐sectional analyses reveal that the main effect is more pronounced among firms with higher external attention and weaker internal governance. Finally, textual analyses characterize blockchain disclosures and blockchain‐related Q&A exchanges by identifying their thematic categories and sentiment distributions. Overall, our findings highlight that corporate blockchain disclosure attracts investor site visits and enhances on‐site communication, which in turn improves long‐term firm value.

papers.title: Government‐Certified Information and Bank Lending to SMEs : Evidence From China's Innovation Points System
papers.abstract: This paper examines whether government‐certified information improves SMEs' access to bank credit. Using China's Innovation Points System (IPS) as a quasi‐natural experiment and a panel of 2128 SMEs from 2016 to 2023, we employ a staggered difference‐in‐differences design. We find that IPS significantly increases firms' bank borrowing by 7.58% relative to the sample mean. The effect is stronger for firms with greater bank‐firm information asymmetry, weaker financial profiles, and stronger innovation capacity. Overall, the results are consistent with the view that government‐certified information improves lenders' assessment of borrowers, thereby reducing credit frictions and enhancing credit allocation.

papers.title: Correction to ‘Tax Authority Governance and Corporate Internal Control Quality’
Earnings Call Tone and Investors' Reliance on Mandatory Disclosures
papers.abstract: This study examines whether the tone of earnings conference calls is associated with investors' subsequent use of firms' mandatory disclosure filings. Using conference call transcripts and EDGAR web traffic data from 2007 to 2016, I find that more positive conference call tone is followed by lower subsequent requests for firms' periodic filings. This relation persists after controlling for firm characteristics, earnings news, analyst following, institutional ownership and leverage, and remains robust in matched sample and weather‐based analyses. I further find that more positive tone is associated with lower implied volatility after the call, consistent with lower perceived uncertainty. The relation between tone and subsequent EDGAR search is also stronger when analyst following and leverage are higher, consistent with a greater role for managerial communication when external scrutiny and verification incentives are stronger. Overall, the findings link voluntary managerial communication to investors' subsequent use of mandatory disclosures.

papers.title: AI Disclosure, Signal Quality and Washing: Evidence From Chinese Listed Firms
papers.abstract: Using Chinese A‐share listed firms from 2016 to 2024, we examine whether Firm‐Specific AI Disclosure predicts subsequent observable AI activity and when disclosure becomes disconnected from action. AI disclosure is most consistently associated with future patenting, while evidence for hiring and broader capital investment is shorter‐lived, supporting an informative‐but‐imperfect signal interpretation. We define AI washing as multidimensional disclosure–action mismatch and find that greater mismatch is associated with AI‐specific stock‐exchange scrutiny. However, inquiry is not followed by broad and persistent realignment: fewer than half of classifiable responses meet our Substantive‐Evidence threshold, consistent with a Detection–Correction Gap.

papers.title: Supply Chain Digital Transformation Misalignment and Supplier Greenwashing: A Dual‐Path Perspective
papers.abstract: Supply chain digital transformation often progresses unevenly across upstream and downstream partners, creating digital transformation misalignment. Drawing on the ability‐motivation‐opportunity (AMO) framework, this study examines how such misalignment affects supplier greenwashing and develops a dual‐path perspective to explain how different directions of digital asymmetry shape supplier responses. Using data on Chinese supply‐chain relationships, we find that supply chain digital transformation misalignment significantly increases supplier greenwashing. Further analyses reveal two distinct behavioural pathways. When suppliers lag behind customers in digital maturity, digital capability constraints limit their ability to undertake and substantiate substantive environmental actions, while relational and transactional pressures increase the incentives to demonstrate environmental responsibility, giving rise to a capability‐constrained symbolic response. In contrast, when suppliers outperform customers in digital maturity, superior information‐processing and information‐control capabilities can weaken customer monitoring and verification, creating opportunities for information‐enabled strategic decoupling. We further identify three mechanisms through which digital transformation misalignment facilitates supplier greenwashing: supply chain information asymmetry, transactional pressure and supervision gaps. In addition, buyer dependency and industry environmental sensitivity amplify the effect of digital transformation misalignment, whereas environmental regulation mitigates it. This study contributes to the supply chain sustainability literature by conceptualizing digital transformation misalignment as a form of sustainability governance imbalance and by demonstrating how different configurations of ability, motivation, and opportunity can generate supplier greenwashing through distinct behavioural pathways. The findings also provide implications for strengthening environmental information governance and monitoring in digitally fragmented supply networks.

papers.title: False Green, True Damage: The Erosion of Supplier Sustainability Through Greenwashing Spillovers in Supply Chains
papers.abstract: Using matched supplier–client data of Chinese A‐share listed companies (2009–2024), we examine how client greenwashing affects suppliers' green total factor productivity (GTFP). We find that client greenwashing significantly suppresses suppliers' GTFP, indicating that downstream firms' selective environmental communication can translate into real efficiency losses in upstream green production. This effect mainly operates through a weakened information environment and reduced supplier green efforts. Further analyses show that the effect is stronger when dependence asymmetry is more pronounced or more difficult to mitigate, namely when clients have greater market influence, when client information transparency is lower, or when suppliers have a lower degree of digital transformation. Our findings reveal that selective environmental communication generates spillover effects beyond disclosing firms, adversely impacting suppliers' green development.

papers.title: Investor Perspectives on Human Capital Disclosures: Australian Evidence
papers.abstract: This study investigates how Australian institutional and retail investors perceive, assess and utilise human capital information. Surveys of 100 and interviews with 11 investors indicate high perceived relevance but limited reported integration of human capital information in decision‐making. Institutional investors emphasised qualitative assessment and engagement, while retail investors relied on reputational cues. Participants expressed dissatisfaction with current disclosures and sought standardised, detailed and comparable metrics. The study extends sustainability disclosure research by highlighting investor‐related barriers and the specific disclosure improvements they seek, with implications for standard setters, regulators and preparers aiming to improve the decision‐usefulness of human capital reporting.

papers.title: Correction to ‘ CEO Organizational Identification and Corporate Innovation Investment’
Information Disclosure Transformation in the Digital Economy: The Role of Digital Infrastructure in Visual Disclosure
papers.abstract: We investigate how digital infrastructure development affects corporate visual disclosure, distinguishing between discretionary image‐based formats and structured table‐based formats. Using data on Chinese A‐share‐listed firms from 2009 to 2022, we find that improvements in digital infrastructure are associated with greater use of image‐based visual disclosure in annual reports, whereas we detect no statistically significant association with table‐based visual disclosure. Mechanism analyses show that this relationship is driven by both supply‐side enhancements in firms' organizational capabilities and demand‐side incentives to cater to external users' information‐processing demands, as evidenced by stronger effects among firms with more extensive explicit discussions of digital transformation in their MD&A and higher institutional ownership. We also find that this effect is more pronounced in regions with higher levels of AI computing power development, as well as among firms with a lower propensity for earnings manipulation and fewer financing constraints. This paper expands the theoretical framework for understanding changes in corporate disclosure formats in the digital economy and offers implications for policymakers, investors and firms.

Resolving Human and Machine Disagreements in Auditing Through the Human and Artificial Intelligence Audit Judgment Resolution Framework
papers.abstract: What should auditors do when a technology recommendation conflicts with their judgement? We interviewed 32 auditors from 25 audit firms in Ghana and analysed their retrospective accounts of 52 reported incidents involving AI systems, advanced analytics and automated decision aids. Participants described questioning outputs, comparing them with other evidence, consulting colleagues or specialists, and redoing analyses before accepting or overriding recommendations. Their accounts linked these responses to the stakes of the decision, the knowledge available to each source, previous experience with the tool, accountability and hierarchy. The Human–AI Audit Judgment Resolution (HAJR) framework brings these patterns together and distinguishes the scrutiny considered necessary from the practical ability to carry it out. It suggests that firms should enable auditors to question outputs and explain both acceptance and rejection. The framework supports theory development; the accounts do not independently establish actual team processes, correct decisions or improved audit quality.

papers.title: Strategising in Auditing: A Strategy‐as‐Practice Approach
papers.abstract: The issue of how auditors strategise in their work has been discussed in the literature, often in relation to specific issues, such as clients, fraud and independence. In this paper, we adopt a more general and explorative perspective to understand strategising in auditing from a strategy‐as‐practice (SAP) perspective. That means that we identify and explain strategising activities of auditors within a professional work context. Based on a case study of auditing processes in Swedish audit firms, we contend that strategising is an individual micro‐level activity and that auditors strategise in relation to standards, software systems and quality control. They do so in various ways and for various reasons, for example, due to a perceived lack of clarity and relevance in the International Standards on Auditing (ISA), inappropriate or misleading guidance in software systems, and a desire to appear as having done more than formally required in relation to quality controls. The article contributes through offering a deeper understanding of how and why auditors strategise within auditing processes.

papers.title: The Business Risk Audit Redux
papers.abstract: In the 1990's, prior to the twin audit scandals of Enron and WorldCom that preceded the Sarbanes‐Oxley Act of 2002, most large audit firms were actively redesigning their audit methodology to better reflect the link between the business risk of a client and the risk of an audit. These methodological innovations were generally referred to as business risk auditing (BRA). The regulatory intervention of SOX caused firms to rethink this approach, but the concepts of BRA continued to inform new auditing standards (e.g., ISA 315). In this essay I argue that the increasing complexity of business and the economy we witness today justifies reconsideration and reworking of these concepts to address a set expanding and increasingly complex risks where authoritative audit guidance may be lacking. I discuss three examples: (1) the expanding subject matter subject to assurance, (2) the transformative effect of technology on information processing and decision making and (3) the blurring of organizational boundaries as more of a company's activities occur in a complex network of strategic relationships.

papers.title: Audit Team Paradox‐in‐Virtuality and Audit Quality Threatening Behaviour
papers.abstract: This study investigates the association between audit team virtuality and audit quality‐threatening behaviour (AQTB). Although virtuality theory suggests that high virtuality can hinder team interactions, virtuality‐in‐paradox theory shows such tools can simultaneously create isolation and efficiency, reduce interpersonal bias and empower timely task completion. This suggests that structural and perceived aspects of virtuality have a more complex influence on team behaviour. Paradox‐in‐virtuality theory is applied to explain how virtuality affects audit team behaviour. Data were collected from 335 auditors across 185 audit team engagements at a Big 4 audit firm using a questionnaire survey. Ordered logistic regression analysis and robustness tests are applied. Results show that audit team virtuality is associated with AQTB. Teams that rely more heavily on communication technologies report higher levels of AQTB, whereas teams experiencing greater synchronicity and higher information quality report lower levels of AQTB. However, the interaction analyses reveal important nuances: When synchronicity occurs together with high technology use, AQTB increases, but when information quality is high, whether combined with technology use or with synchronicity, AQTB becomes less frequent. The consequences are analysed, and future research prospects are discussed. This research contributes to audit quality and audit team literature by identifying determinants of AQTB at the team level. Insights into audit team behaviour are valuable for practitioners adapting to new communication technologies. Contributions are made to team virtuality research and behavioural outcomes by testing its three dimensions in professional audit practice.
