Exploring motivations, challenges and strategic actions in setting Science-based Targets (SBTs) by New Zealand firms
papers.abstract: This study critically examines the extent to which corporate emissions reduction targets are grounded in science-based principles. It explores the motivations, challenges and strategies that shape such target setting. The study adopts a mixed-methods design. It combines longitudinal content analysis of over 500 organisational reports from New Zealand’s 50 largest listed firms over ten years (2012–2021) with 29 interviews with senior managers from 23 of those firms in 2019. Drawing on achievement goal theory, we identify four distinct clusters of firms: mastery approach, performance approach, mastery avoidance, and performance avoidance, and map each cluster to observable target-setting practices. Mastery avoidance is the most prevalent approach which reflects an absence of science-based targets driven by a lack of know-how, a lack of technology, constraints on the needed changes in assets, or a lack of external guidance. The next common cluster is a performance approach where firms manage stakeholders’ relationships through supplier engagement targets, participation in policy processes, and the use of third-party verification to enhance credibility. Performance avoidance is much less popular which is characterised by reliance on offsetting; the adoption of feasible targets aligned with current capabilities and cautious external disclosure. Finally, mastery-oriented firms develop absolute science-based targets and undertake substantive operational and business model change to achieve their targets. Overall, the study contributes to accounting and sustainability literatures by explaining how firms adopt (or avoid) setting science-based targets, and how they operationalise these targets to make progress on their climate mitigation journey.

papers.title: The configurational logic of management control: exploring pathways to offshoring performance
papers.abstract: This study investigates how management control (MC) practices—formal and informal controls—and contextual factors, including trust, cultural competency, and relationship continuity, combine in configurations associated with offshoring performance. Existing research has largely examined control mechanisms in isolation, and prior work has not yet offered a configurational perspective on how MC practices and contextual factors jointly shape offshoring performance. Using data from 55 Swedish firms engaged in offshore outsourcing and applying fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA), the study identifies multiple configurations of MC practices and contextual factors linked to offshoring success and offshoring failure. The findings reveal two distinct pathways to offshoring success. The first is a hybrid MC package that combines outcome control with informal controls, namely social control and self-control, alongside contextual factors. The second is a relational MC package characterized by the joint presence of social control, competence trust, goodwill trust, and relationship continuity in the absence of formal controls. In contrast, the configurations associated with offshoring failure are consistently marked by the absence of social control, goodwill trust, cultural competency, and relationship continuity, demonstrating that failure is not simply the inverse of success. The study contributes to the MC package literature by showing how MC practices and contextual factors combine in offshoring relationships. It also clarifies the role of contextual factors in offshoring performance and extends research on offshoring failure by showing causal asymmetry between success and failure configurations.

papers.title: How does the net income reconciliation from IFRS to US GAAP affect audit report lag?
papers.abstract: Purpose This paper examines whether the number of reconciling line items in the reconciliation, the absolute magnitude and the income-effect of the adjustments, of net income from International Financial Reporting Standards to United States Generally Accepted Accounting Principles affect audit report lag. Design/methodology/approach The sample consists of European Union firms listed in the USA for the period from 2005 to 2007 that prepared the reconciliation of net income in Form 20F. An audit report lag model is used to study the effect of the audit of the note on audit completion. An audit fee model is used as a supplementary tool. Findings This paper reports that audit report lag is longer for more reconciling line items or larger absolute magnitude of the net income adjustments and shorter for more income-increasing adjustments. Audit fees are increasing in the number of reconciling line items and in the absolute magnitude of the adjustments but decreasing in income-increasing effect of the adjustments. Research limitations/implications Generalisation should be done cautiously because of the small sample size and the fact that all sample firms were audited by a Big 4 auditor. Originality/value In its suggestion to remove the reconciliation requirement, the Securities and Exchange Commission argued that the removal would facilitate capital formation by making financial statements available earlier. However, it did not estimate how quickly such statements would be available. This paper provides evidence that suggests that financial statements would be available earlier because the audit of the reconciliation note takes time and hence, its removal would save time. This evidence is more informative than the evidence on the removal itself because it shows how the reconciliation affects audit completion but not just whether it affects the completion or not.

papers.title: Big 4 office agglomeration and asymmetric pricing dynamics in local audit markets
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how the geographic agglomeration of Big 4 audit offices within metropolitan areas influences audit pricing across auditor tiers. The authors conceptualize Big 4 agglomeration, measured as the ratio of Big 4 to total audit offices within a market, as a spatial dimension of audit market structure that captures both competitive intensity and knowledge spillovers. The study investigates whether this agglomeration affects audit fees differently for clients of Big 4 and non-Big 4 auditors. Design/methodology/approach Using US public company data from 2004 to 2017, the authors estimate audit fee regressions incorporating a measure of Big 4 office agglomeration within each metropolitan statistical area. The analysis distinguishes between Big 4 and non-Big 4 clients, includes extensive controls and uses entropy balancing to assess the robustness of the findings. Additional analyses examine changes in Big 4 office agglomeration, exclude the financial crisis period and consider alternative geographic market definitions to assess the sensitivity of the results. The authors also interact Big 4 office agglomeration with spatial market-share distance measures to explore the mechanisms underlying the asymmetric pricing effects. Findings The authors find that greater Big 4 agglomeration is associated with lower audit fees for Big 4 clients but higher fees for non-Big 4 clients. These results are consistent with greater Big 4 office agglomeration intensifying intra-tier competition while potentially facilitating learning and reputation spillovers that enhance non-Big 4 auditors’ capabilities and pricing power. These opposite associations are robust across alternative fee measures and several additional specifications. Practical implications High geographic agglomeration of Big 4 offices may intensify rivalry within the top tier while strengthening smaller firms through capability spillovers. These findings inform regulatory oversight, competition policy and audit firms’ strategic location decisions. Originality/value This study introduces the concept of Big 4 agglomeration as a novel, spatially grounded measure of audit market structure. By demonstrating asymmetric pricing effects across auditor tiers, the study bridges auditing research with agglomeration theory and industrial organization. It provides new insight into how local geography, competition and inter-organizational learning interact to shape audit pricing in the local audit markets.

papers.title: Speaking up and being heard: the impact of communication on auditor integrity actions
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine the impact of communication (i.e. speaking up and being heard) on auditor integrity actions. Integrity is a fundamental principle for professional accountants, and it is warranted to investigate factors that may affect auditor integrity actions. Design/methodology/approach This study uses data from survey responses of auditors working in audit firms in Norway. The main regression analysis that tests the association between auditor integrity actions and communication is based on 61 responses from auditors who are below the rank of partners. Findings This study finds evidence for the positive impacts of subordinate auditors’ willingness to speak up and feeling of being heard on their integrity actions. Interestingly, when these two factors are considered, the negative impact of auditors’ workload on their integrity actions either greatly decreases or becomes insignificant. Research limitations/implications This study’s limitations include small sample size, potential biases in participants’ interpretation of survey questions and a focus on associations rather than causal relationships, among others. Practical implications This study provides important insights for audit firms and regulators in terms of taking actions to promote effective communication within audit firms to uphold auditor integrity actions. Social implications This study highlights the importance of social interactions within audit teams, suggesting that strong interpersonal relationships and audit firm communication culture can improve auditor integrity actions and, ultimately, enhance audit quality. Originality/value This study’s originality lies in its investigation of auditor communication on their integrity actions – an area that has received limited attention despite its critical importance to audit quality and public trust – offering a novel contribution to the audit literature.

papers.title: Auditor switching under COVID-19 pandemic: evidence from China
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine whether and how the COVID-19 pandemic altered firms’ auditor switching behavior. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on crisis management theory, the authors analyze a panel data set of Chinese A-share listed manufacturing firms from 2016 to 2023 using a propensity score matching–difference-in-differences (PSM–DiD) approach. Findings Pandemic exposure significantly increased auditor switching likelihood. This effect was attenuated by slack resources but amplified when the incumbent auditor was a large audit firm, suggesting that crisis-induced switching reflects strategic adaptation shaped by internal resource endowments and external relational constraints. Practical implications Managers may leverage auditor switching as a crisis adaptation strategy, though such decisions carry audit quality risks. Regulators should monitor elevated switching rates during crises as potential indicators of governance stress. Originality/value This paper contributes to the literature by empirically investigating auditor switching as a strategic crisis response. By integrating crisis management theory with established auditor switching perspectives, it complements the “auditor-side” COVID-19 literature with a “client-side” perspective and identifies boundary conditions governing firms’ crisis responses.

papers.title: Guardians of governance: the role of auditor industry specialization in mitigating corporate misconduct through internal controls
papers.abstract: Purpose This study examines the impact of statutory auditor industry specialization on corporate misconduct in China’s A-share market, with a specific focus on the mediating role of internal control quality in mitigating corporate misconduct. Design/methodology/approach Using a sample of 3,794 firms (2010-2022), we apply fixed-effects regression models and a two-stage least squares (2SLS) approach to address potential endogeneity. We quantify auditor industry specialization using market share, while the occurrence and frequency of regulatory violations are used to measure corporate misconduct. Findings The results show that auditors with industry specialization significantly reduce both the likelihood and frequency of corporate misconduct. Furthermore, internal control quality serves as a significant mediating mechanism in the relationship between auditor industry specialization and corporate misconduct. These findings highlight the role of industry specialized auditors as vital external governance agents, particularly in firms with concentrated ownership or those operating in highly competitive industries. Practical implications This study highlights policy implications for regulators and policymakers, recommending the development of auditor industry specialization through certification programs and stricter industry-specific auditing standards. Firms should engage industry-specialized auditors and invest in resources and training to improve the quality of internal controls. Originality/value This research significantly contributes to the corporate governance and auditing literature by highlighting that auditor industry specialization serves as a key external disciplinary mechanism that enhances the effectiveness of internal control. It also contributes to agency and resource-based theories by highlighting the critical role of auditor industry specialization and internal control in detecting and preventing corporate misconduct.

papers.title: Audit committees and climate risk disclosure: a transformer-based textual analysis approach
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine whether audit committee (AC) attributes are associated with the extent of climate risk disclosure in mandated US annual reports, distinguishing between physical- and transition-risk discussion in 10-K Item 1A (Risk Factors). Design/methodology/approach Using S&P 500 firms, the study extracts Item 1A from 10-K filings and applies a transformer-based NLP classifier (ClimateBERT) to score firm-year physical- and transition-risk disclosure. Multiple regression models and alternative proxies are used to test the robustness of results. Findings The results show that AC independence, gender diversity and expertise are associated with higher physical- and transition-risk disclosure, consistent with stronger monitoring and closer review of climate-related narratives in 10-K filings. Longer committee tenure is linked to lower disclosure, suggesting that familiarity with management may soften scrutiny over time. The presence of an AC is also associated with higher disclosure. These results are stronger in carbon-intensive sectors and remain stable across multiple robustness tests. Research limitations/implications The study is limited to large US non-financial firms (S&P 500), which may restrict generalizability. The dependent variables are disclosure-based measures derived from textual classification of Item 1A and reflect how risks are communicated rather than underlying exposure. Practical implications Boards, AC chairs and investors can expect AC composition to shape the depth and clarity of climate-risk discussion in 10-K risk factors. Independence, gender mix and expertise are linked to fuller narratives that help users assess physical hazards and transition pressures. Regulators may also view AC features as part of the reporting system that helps explain cross-firm differences in climate-risk communication under a common US regime. Originality/value The study connects AC design to climate-risk disclosure in Form 10-K filings by using transformer-based text analytics that separate physical from transition risk within Item 1A. This provides fresh evidence on how reporting oversight relates to emerging-risk narratives and offers a scalable method for governance–disclosure research.

papers.title: Diversity in Accounting: A Systematic Review of Gender and Age in Corporate Governance and Firm Performance
papers.abstract: This structured review synthesizes recent research on age and gender diversity in leadership roles central to financial reporting and assurance. It examines how leadership composition relates to corporate governance mechanisms and firm-level outcomes, including earnings quality, restatements, internal controls, audit quality, risk-taking, cost of capital, and litigation. Women and older professionals in positions of formal authority are associated with more conservative reporting, stronger monitoring, and higher stakeholder confidence. However, these associations depend on institutional context and on whether these leaders hold substantive decision-making power. Finally, the review discusses possible mechanisms linking leadership diversity to oversight and performance. It also identifies gaps in the literature related to intersectionality, positional authority, and underexplored domains such as audit firm governance. The review discusses implications for boards, audit committees, professional bodies, and regulators concerned with the public interest. Data Availability: All studies and sources synthesized in the review are publicly available from the publishers cited in the reference list. JEL Classifications: M14; G34; M41; L25.

papers.title: The dual effect of corporate innovation culture on digital mergers and acquisitions
papers.abstract: Purpose Research has largely examined digital mergers and acquisitions (M&A) outcomes and external drivers while overlooking corporate culture. This study aims to investigate how innovation culture shapes firms’ make-or-buy choices in digital M&A. Design/methodology/approach The authors use Word2Vec and sentiment-weighted management discussion and analysis text to measure innovation culture. Digital M&A is identified from target firms’ business scopes and industry codes. Logistic regressions and robustness tests assess the proposed relationships. Findings Stronger innovation culture promotes digital M&A, partly through greater risk-taking. Its effect is strongest during the introduction stage but insignificant during decline. Digital M&A also partially transmits the effect of innovation culture into greater post-merger digital patent quantity and citation-based quality. Practical implications Firms should foster open, collaborative innovation cultures; investors should consider cultural capital alongside financial measures; and policymakers should encourage organisational innovation and strategic resilience. Originality/value This study develops a text-based measure of innovation culture and links it to digital M&A decisions and post-merger digital research and development outcomes.

papers.title: Does firm life cycle affect the dynamics of intellectual capital and earnings management practices? Evidence from seven emerging (E7) economies
papers.abstract: Purpose This research aims to address the inconclusive outcomes of the intellectual capital (IC) and earnings management (EM) relationship by incorporating the firm life cycle into the research domain. This study examined this IC and EM dynamics in seven emerging economies (E7), e.g. Brazil, China, India, Indonesia, Mexico, Russia and Turkey. Design/methodology/approach This study examined the relationship using the standard error–corrected Driscoll & Kraay panel regression models on a sample of 2,610 nonfinancial firms from 2011 to 2023. This research explores both linear and curvilinear relationships among IC and EM practices at different stages of the firm life cycle. This study performed robustness checks using system GMM and propensity score matching models. Findings The findings assert that IC reduces both accrual earnings management (AEM) and real earnings management (REM), except for income-decreasing REM. However, the curvilinear relationship claims that low to moderate levels of IC constrain EM practices, whereas excessive investment in IC increases EM. In addition, this study finds that firms are vulnerable to EM practices at the introduction and decline stages. However, investment in IC constrains both AEM and REM at different life cycle stages, except for the introduction stage. Practical implications This study suggests that management and regulatory bodies may prioritize IC investments to protect the earnings quality of firms, especially when they are at the introduction or decline stages. Originality/value This study makes a novel contribution by examining the connection between IC and EM practices (both accrual and real) at different stages of the firm life cycle in E7 nations.

papers.title: What drives bias and accuracy in management earnings forecasts? A meta-analysis of 58 studies
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to consolidate and evaluate what is known about the determinants of management earnings forecast (MF) quality. More broadly, it aims to improve understanding of when and why management forecasts provide higher-quality guidance to capital-market participants by linking prior evidence to theoretical mechanisms such as forecast ability, managerial opportunism, environmental uncertainty and governance and monitoring. Design/methodology/approach A meta-analysis of 58 empirical studies published between 1992 and 2021 is performed. Reported associations, including correlations and effect sizes derived from reported test statistics, are converted to comparable effect sizes and aggregated using the Hunter and Schmidt approach, with robustness checks based on random-effects models, heterogeneity diagnostics, meta-regressions and publication-bias tests. Findings MF quality varies systematically with forecast attributes and firm conditions, but effect sizes differ across determinants and outcomes. Forecast horizon and financial performance show the strongest associations: longer horizons are associated with lower accuracy and higher optimistic bias, while stronger performance is associated with higher accuracy and lower optimistic bias. Firm size is positively related to accuracy and negatively related to optimistic bias, though associations are smaller. Firm growth shows no reliable link with accuracy and only a small link with bias. Leverage is weakly associated with lower accuracy and has no stable relationship with bias. Research limitations/implications The synthesis is constrained to determinants reported frequently in comparable forms, leaving less frequently measured constructs outside the meta-analytic scope. Because the literature search ends in 2021 and the underlying samples end in 2020, the analysis does not capture more recent regulatory, market and technology-related developments. Practical implications Users of earnings guidance should adjust credibility assessments for horizon, performance and firm size when interpreting management forecasts. Social implications The manuscript does not focus on societal outcomes in the narrow sense, but an improved understanding of when management guidance is more/less reliable can contribute indirectly to better capital allocation and reduced information asymmetry. Originality/value This study delivers the first meta-analysis of key determinants of MF accuracy and bias, links findings to an integrative theoretical framework, examines cross-study differences via moderator tests and offers practical guidance for evaluating forecasts.

papers.title: Shadow banking regulation and corporate tax avoidance: empirical evidence from China
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine the impact of shadow banking regulation on corporate tax avoidance and the underlying mechanisms driving this effect. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on a firm-level sample of Chinese A-share listed companies covering the period 2010–2024, this paper uses China’s 2017 shadow banking regulations as a quasi-natural experiment and adopts a difference-in-differences framework to identify the causal effect of shadow banking regulation on corporate tax avoidance. The authors further explore the underlying transmission mechanisms and cross-sectional heterogeneity of this relationship. Findings Shadow banking regulation significantly reduces corporate tax avoidance. Improvements in corporate information transparency and stronger governance constraints are two important channels through which this effect operates. Further analysis shows that the negative effect of shadow banking regulation on tax avoidance is more pronounced among firms with greater tax-avoidance opportunities, tighter financing constraints, weaker internal governance, weaker regional legal institutions and lower product-market competition. Originality/value This study contributes to the literature on the economic consequences of shadow banking regulation and the determinants of corporate tax avoidance. It provides new evidence that financial regulation can shape corporate tax behavior by improving the transparency of financing arrangements and strengthening governance. The findings show that the effects of shadow banking regulation extend beyond financing and resource allocation.

papers.title: Accounting conservatism and SEO announcement returns: the role of culture and institutions
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine the influence of culture and institutions on the relationship between accounting conservatism and seasoned equity offering (SEO) announcement returns. It aims to assess whether a composite measure of accounting value of conservatism (AVC) and the Rule of Law Index moderate this relationship in an international context. Design/methodology/approach Using a sample of SEOs issued in 35 countries from 2002 to 2021, the authors investigate how culture and institutional factors interact with accounting conservatism. The authors focus on the moderating effect of AVC and the Rule of Law Index on the association between conservatism and market reactions to SEO announcements. Findings The authors find that AVC explains part of the variability in the association between accounting conservatism and SEO announcement returns. The positive effect of conservatism on market reaction found in the USA is not generalizable to other countries. Moreover, both conditional and unconditional conservatism are positively associated with SEO announcement returns in countries with high AVC. Practical implications These results emphasize the role of cultural values in shaping how investors perceive conservative accounting, which can inform managers and policymakers in tailoring financial communication strategies to cultural contexts. Originality/value This study contributes to SEO costs and accounting conservatism by showing that the relationship between conservatism and SEO announcement returns varies internationally, driven in part by cultural preferences for conservatism.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence and corporate green transformation: evidence from China’s A-share listed firms
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how artificial intelligence (AI) adoption contributes to corporate green transformation. It analyses the mediating roles of green technological innovation and human capital upgrading, the moderating roles of organisational resilience and environmental regulation and the heterogeneous effects across industrial and regional contexts. Design/methodology/approach This study uses panel data on Chinese A-share listed non-financial firms from 2008 to 2023. Fixed-effects regressions, instrumental-variable estimation, propensity score matching, mediation analysis, interaction models and subgroup analyses are used to examine the relationship between AI adoption and corporate green transformation, its transmission mechanisms, boundary conditions and contextual heterogeneity. Findings AI adoption is positively associated with corporate green transformation, and the result remains robust to alternative measures and endogeneity tests. Green technological innovation and human capital upgrading partially mediate this relationship, while organisational resilience and environmental regulation strengthen it. The positive relationship is statistically significant among firms in non-heavily polluting industries, firms in eastern and western China and firms in non-resource-based cities, but not in the corresponding comparison groups. Originality/value This study extends recent evidence on the environmental effects of AI by explaining how AI adoption is converted into firm-level green transformation and why this process varies across firms and locations. It provides an integrated account of the technological, workforce, organisational, institutional and structural conditions that shape the environmental value of AI adoption.

papers.title: Recent Central Bank Losses in Historical Perspective
papers.abstract: To what extent are recent central bank losses unprecedented? To answer this question, this article briefly surveys a number of historical episodes in which significant central bank losses actually occurred. It shows that central bank losses have not been rare in history, and that they have not necessarily impaired central banks’ independence from government. However, recent losses are unprecedented in that they originate from central banks’ exposure to interest rate risk. Such an exposure is the result of the combined lifting of reserve requirements and introduction of remunerated deposit facilities, which has made central banks’ liabilities structurally costly for the first time in history.

papers.journal: Accounting, Economics and Law: A Convivium
papers.title: The European Supervisory System for Crowdfunding Service Providers: Regulatory Stratification and Critical Issues in its Implementation Within the Italian Legal Systems
papers.abstract: The adoption of a unified European regulatory framework for crowdfunding seeks to address the challenges arising from the pre-existing regulatory fragmentation among Member States by establishing harmonized requirements concerning the provision of crowdfunding services, the organization, authorization, and supervision of service providers, as well as the operation of platforms, transparency obligations, and marketing communications, while ensuring consistent mechanisms for investor protection. This paper focuses on the European supervisory architecture applicable to crowdfunding service providers, with particular attention to its distinctive features vis-à-vis the role assigned to national competent authorities, in contrast with the initially envisaged framework under which ESMA was relegated to a largely marginal role. The principal specificity of the system, however, lies in the interaction and partial overlap between European norms and national legal frameworks governing the sector, notwithstanding that the European crowdfunding regulation constitutes a fully binding and directly applicable instrument in each Member State pursuant to art. 288 TFEU. Considering these features, the study aims to evaluate the extent of discretion afforded to national authorities, through an examination of the implementation process in Italy, which serves as an illustrative case of regulatory expansion resulting from the coexistence of multiple national competent authorities.

papers.journal: Accounting, Economics and Law: A Convivium
papers.title: Frontmatter
Crisis or opportunity? Reviewing the dynamics of intellectual capital, financial distress and earnings management practices in emerging economies
papers.abstract: Purpose This study examines the impact of intellectual capital (IC) on the financial distress (FD) of firms in seven emerging (E7) economies, e.g. Brazil, China, India, Indonesia, Mexico, Russia and Turkey, with a special reference to earnings management (EM) practices. By doing so, the research reconciles the contradictory outcomes on the dynamics among IC, FD, and EM practices. Design/methodology/approach We have used the standard error-corrected Driscoll and Kraay panel regression models and explored both linear and curvilinear relationships among the IC, FD and EM. The study checked the robustness of the findings by employing both alternative proxies and two-stage least squares (2SLS) models. Findings IC helps in reducing financial distress, suggesting that a stronger IC contributes to better financial stability. Firms use EM practices like accrual and discretionary expenses when they are in a financially distressed zone or crisis scenario, while financially stable firms use real earnings management (REM) through sales manipulation practices. The findings also show that the use of IC prevents firms from practicing EM even if they are in a distressed situation. The direction of EM reveals that IC-oriented firms tend to avoid income-increasing REM, while distressed firms use income-increasing REM as an opportunity to enhance their bottom-line figure. Practical implications The study brings managerial and policy implications for promoting investment in IC to reduce the financial distress and constrain EM. Originality/value The study holds a unique positioning as it conducts an empirical study on the interconnection among IC, FD and EM practices in seven emerging economies.

papers.title: Professional workforce composition and compensation in accounting firms: evidence from Taiwan
papers.abstract: Purpose This study examines whether professional workforce composition is conditionally associated with firm-level aggregate compensation and benefits (CB) in Taiwanese certified public accounting (CPA) firms and whether the associations differ between partnership firms and sole proprietorships. Design/methodology/approach The study uses de-identified firm-level data from the 2019 Survey Report on the Service Industry of CPA Firms. The final sample comprises 1,134 firms. Ordinary least squares models are estimated separately by organizational form. Additional count-based, separate-ratio and incremental workforce-share analyses are used to assess sensitivity to alternative workforce specifications. Findings The joint ratio models show positive associations between several professional-service ratios and firm-level aggregate CB. However, the supplemental analyses show that these associations are sensitive to the measurement and joint inclusion of interdependent workforce-share variables. The evidence is therefore interpreted as composition-based firm-level associations rather than as robust independent headcount effects or individual wage premiums. Research limitations/implications The cross-sectional design cannot resolve reverse causality between staffing composition and compensation budgets, and the firm-level compensation measure does not estimate individual employee pay. The results should be read as conditional associations that identify how workforce configuration, organizational form and aggregate compensation governance are related. Practical implications The implications are differentiated across large partnership firms, small sole proprietorships, regulators and industry associations. They emphasize cautious use of staffing-ratio evidence, clearer separation of employee compensation from owner distributions and more detailed industry data on functional staff counts, ranks, full-time equivalents and compensation components. Originality/value The study treats firm-level aggregate CB as a strategic outcome related to workforce configuration, while explicitly showing that the interpretation depends on whether workforce allocation is measured as proportions, absolute headcounts or incrementally introduced staffing shares.

papers.title: NRBV's strategic capabilities and SDG disclosure: Does this disclosure enhance financial performance?
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to extend the sustainable development goals (SDG) disclosure literature by examining the influence of natural resource-based view (NRBV) strategic capabilities, namely pollution prevention, green product innovation and environmental certification, on SDG disclosure practices among Indonesian companies. It also investigates the association between this disclosure and financial performance. Design/methodology/approach This study uses Indonesian companies listed in Indonesia Stock Exchange (IDX) for the period 2021 to 2024, comprising 1,256 company-year observations from 314 companies. All data for the variables are collected from annual and sustainability reports and analyzed using panel regression. Findings This study demonstrates that NRBV-based strategic capabilities, such as pollution prevention, green product innovation and environmental certification, significantly enhance companies' SDG disclosure. However, such disclosure is associated with lower financial performance due to the substantial costs required to support SDG-related activities. Practical implications The findings of this study provide practical implications for regulators as the commitment for achieving the SDG can be actualized through stricter sustainability regulations. It can be used to encourage companies to integrate strategic capabilities provided by NRBV into business operations. Originality/value This study extends the existing literature on SDG disclosure by shifting the focus from commonly examined governance and ownership determinants to the role of NRBV's strategic capabilities. It further contributes by examining the implications of SDG disclosure for companies' financial performance within an emerging market country context like Indonesia. This study also provides complementary evidence to prior studies predominantly conducted in developed countries.

papers.title: Bankruptcy system reform and shadow banking activities of non-financial enterprises: evidence from China
papers.abstract: Purpose Bankruptcy system reform is an effective measure to improve judicial efficiency in bankruptcy proceedings and protect the legitimate rights and interests of creditors. It plays an important role in promoting the development of credit markets. Design/methodology/approach Based on a quasi-natural experiment of establishing bankruptcy court in China, this paper examines the impact of the establishment of bankruptcy court on shadow banking activities of non-financial enterprises, using a multi-period difference-in-differences model with China's A-share listed enterprises as the research object from 2016 to 2022. Findings The findings show that the establishment of bankruptcy court increases the scale of shadow banking activities of non-financial enterprises. Furthermore, enhancing creditor protection and increasing management risk preference play important mechanism effect. Bankruptcy law enforcement efficiency demonstrates a strong moderating effect. Originality/value This study provides empirical evidence for evaluating the quality and effectiveness of bankruptcy system reform and offers instructive insights for activating informal finance, regulating shadow banking activities and maintaining financial market stability.

papers.title: Intergenerational Succession and Family Firms’ AI Engagement
Practitioner Perspectives: Private Equity Investment Influence on Audit Practice through Firm Leadership
papers.abstract: The accounting profession is undergoing a major shift as private equity (PE) investment accelerates and Alternative Practice Structures (APS) expand. This paper provides a qualitative snapshot of these changes through interview insights from practitioners: (1) two assurance partners at PE-backed national firms, (2) a PE investor, and (3) a strategic advisor from a firm that has declined PE funding. Seeking a short-term return on investment, PE management’s aim to rapidly increase firm value affects the audit practice through technological innovations, more audit engagements at lower costs, and the avid pursuit of non-attest services. The assurance partners laud these audit practice adaptations, whereas the PE investor cautions against only short-term priorities and the strategic advisor warns of independence concerns. The insights from these practitioners, coupled with recent regulatory actions, industry events, and relevant research, establish a foundation for PE investment effects on audit practice as well as future empirical work. JEL Classifications: M41; M42; M48.

papers.journal: International Journal of Accounting and Information Management
papers.title: CEO sustainability activism and earnings management in European firms
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine the association between media coverage of CEOs’ activism in sustainability and earnings management (EM), thereby assessing whether CEO sustainability visibility is related to the quality of financial reporting. Design/methodology/approach The authors analyze 1,580 firm-year observations from 161 European nonfinancial firms listed in the S&P 350 Europe Index between 2014 and 2022. CEO sustainability activism was tracked through LexisNexis media coverage, while EM was measured via proxies for accrual-based (AEM) and real earnings (REM) management. Models are estimated using pooled ordinary least squares regressions with clustered standard errors. Findings Media visibility of CEO sustainability activism is significantly associated with lower levels of REM, but unrelated to AEM in the full sample. This association is stronger for longer-tenured CEOs, while co-opted CFOs weaken it. For female CEOs, greater visibility is also associated with lower levels of AEM. Practical implications The findings of this study are consistent with the view that media scrutiny may operate as a reputational governance mechanism that complements regulation and investor oversight. For boards, aligning executive communication on sustainability with financial reporting integrity is vital for avoiding reputational risks. Regulators and investors may consider CEO media exposure as an additional signal when assessing the credibility of commitments to sustainability, while for managers, visibility in sustainability activism may entail heightened accountability and reinforce the need for consistent financial reporting practices. Originality/value By linking CEO sustainability activism, media coverage and EM, this study provides evidence consistent with the view that reputational pressures extend beyond symbolic corporate social responsibility disclosure and are related to core financial reporting practices, offering a novel perspective on transparency and accountability in capital markets.

papers.title: Do different owners matter for environmental and social information disclosure? Evidence from Vietnamese listed companies
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to investigate how ownership structure, both as a composite governance construct and through its individual ownership dimensions, is associated with environmental and social information disclosure (DESI) among Vietnamese listed companies. Design/methodology/approach The study uses panel data from 601 nonfinancial companies listed on the Vietnamese stock market during 2021–2025, representing 3,005 firm-year observations. The study examines the aggregate relationship between ownership structure and DESI using a PCA-derived ownership index, as well as the relationships between five individual ownership dimensions and DESI. FGLS is used as the main estimation method to account for heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation in the panel data, while a fixed-effects model with cluster-robust standard errors is used as an alternative specification to assess the robustness of the main findings. Findings The results show that ownership structure is positively associated with DESI. Among the ownership dimensions, foreign ownership, institutional ownership, state ownership, managerial ownership and ownership concentration all show positive and statistically significant associations with DESI in their respective specifications. These findings suggest that ownership structure functions as a multidimensional governance mechanism for enhancing DESI in Vietnam’s evolving institutional environment, extending stakeholder and legitimacy theories. Given the institutional similarities between Vietnam and many emerging economies, the findings also offer broader implications beyond the Vietnamese context. Research limitations/implications This study focuses on non-financial listed companies in Vietnam during the 2021–2025 period. Future studies may extend the analysis to other industries, countries or governance mechanisms and investigate moderating or mediating factors affecting the relationship between ownership structure and DESI. Future studies should address potential endogeneity and reverse causality using stronger causal identification strategies. Practical implications The findings suggest that companies should strengthen ownership governance by fostering effective monitoring from diverse ownership groups, while policymakers should enhance ownership transparency and sustainability disclosure regulations. Social implications Improved DESI may contribute to greater corporate accountability, enhance stakeholder confidence, support environmental protection and social responsibility and promote sustainable economic development in emerging markets such as Vietnam. Originality/value Unlike previous studies that focused on individual ownership dimensions, this study integrates ownership into a PCA-based composite index while simultaneously examining both the composite and individual ownership effects, providing new evidence from Vietnam that is relevant to emerging markets.

papers.journal: International Journal of Accounting and Information Management
papers.title: Culture shaped conditional accounting conservatism: evidence from US public firms
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine whether corporate culture influences firms’ financial reporting behavior through its impact on conditional accounting conservatism. While prior literature primarily attributes conservatism to external institutional factors, contracting incentives, litigation risk and regulatory pressures, this study investigates whether firm-level cultural values act as internal determinants shaping the timely recognition of economic losses. Design/methodology/approach Using a large panel of US publicly listed firms, the analysis combines machine-learning–based measures of corporate culture developed by Li et al. (2021) with the firm-year C-score framework of Khan and Watts (2009), grounded in the asymmetric timeliness model of Basu (1997). The design evaluates how five cultural dimensions: innovation, integrity, quality, respect and teamwork affect conditional conservatism. Findings Corporate culture significantly influences the timely recognition of economic losses. Cultures emphasizing integrity, quality, respect and teamwork are positively associated with conditional conservatism, suggesting ethical and collaborative environments strengthen internal governance and promote transparent reporting. Conversely, innovation-oriented cultures are negatively associated with conservatism, consistent with greater emphasis on experimentation and risk-taking. Subsample analyses indicate these effects are stronger where cultural values are deeply embedded, and a culture-augmented asymmetric timeliness model confirms that culture enhances earnings’ responsiveness to bad news relative to good news. Originality/value The study links corporate culture to conditional conservatism, identifying culture as an internal governance mechanism in financial reporting. By integrating machine-learning–based cultural measures with established conservatism frameworks, it bridges organizational culture research with traditional accounting models and captures within-country heterogeneity overlooked by national-culture studies.

Artificial intelligence as recurring organizational change: accountability and management control challenges across AI waves
papers.abstract: Purpose Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in organizational decision-making, raising questions about how decision authority, accountability and management control are allocated and maintained. This paper aims to examine why accountability and management control challenges may recur across different technological configurations. It proposes that such challenges can arise when changes in effective decision authority are not accompanied by corresponding clarification of organizational responsibility and opportunities for oversight and intervention. Design/methodology/approach The study adopts a conceptual and interpretive research design based on a historically informed analysis of organizational change. Drawing on literature from management control, governance and organizational studies, it compares four waves of AI-related organizational change: computational decision support as a precursor to organizational AI adoption, followed by expert systems, data-driven and algorithmic management and contemporary AI-enabled environments. The analysis develops a conceptual synthesis of recurring accountability questions across these configurations. Findings The analysis identifies four recurring areas of concern: potential misalignment between effective decision authority and formal responsibility; limitations in decision visibility and traceability; insufficient integration of decision technologies with strategic management control; and governance arrangements that may require adaptation as systems and organizational uses change. These patterns are not presented as inevitable outcomes of AI adoption. Instead, the study proposes authority–responsibility decoupling as a mechanism through which accountability and management control gaps may persist or reemerge under particular organizational conditions. Originality/value The paper contributes to research on accounting and organizational change by connecting contemporary AI governance questions to a longer history of organizational decision technologies. Its wave-based framework distinguishes a precursor phase of computational decision support from subsequent AI adoption and links recurring accountability challenges to decision rights, responsibility, oversight and management control. The resulting conceptual proposition provides a basis for future empirical research and for examining how governance arrangements can be adapted to AI-enabled decision processes.

papers.title: From net show to net zero: conceptualising corporate climate accountability
papers.abstract: Purpose This paper aims to examine how corporate net zero commitments are developed and put into practice and what mechanisms shape their translation into climate accountability in an emerging economy context. It explains how organisations sustain symbolic climate alignment, identifies the mechanisms enabling this pattern to persist and conceptualises the conditions under which climate accountability may shift towards substantive practice. Design/methodology/approach The study draws on 67 semi-structured interviews with managers, regulators, consultants, academics and non-governmental organisations in Indonesia. Using an interpretive qualitative approach, the analysis develops an empirically grounded account of how climate accountability is constructed through organisational processes and institutional conditions. Findings Three mechanisms (scope decoupling, subsidiary silencing and temporal displacement) help sustain symbolic climate alignment through accounting boundaries, governance arrangements and performance management systems. These mechanisms form a relatively stabilised configuration referred to as net show equilibrium. The study develops analytically derived climate accountability pathways (mandate, mobilise, measure, mainstream and monitor) which conceptualise conditions under which accountability may be reconfigured. Credible transition appears to depend on aligned emissions scopes, group-wide accountability and near-term milestones. Research limitations/implications The study is based on cross-sectional qualitative evidence and captures recurring patterns rather than longitudinal change. Practical implications Credible climate accountability appears to depend on changes in organisational routines, roles and control systems rather than disclosure alone. Social implications Selective accountability boundaries and deferred responsibility may have implications for affected communities and environmental governance. Originality/value The paper introduces net show equilibrium and climate accountability pathways to explain how climate accountability is organisationally structured and sustained.

papers.title: Corrigendum: Organizational change factors and their impact on artificial intelligence adoption in management accounting
Management accountants’ identity in the Global South under digital and sustainability transformation: evidence from Asia Pacific
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how management accountants in the Global South reconstruct their identities and negotiate legitimacy while navigating digital transformation, sustainability mandates and the structural constraints of institutional asymmetry. Design/methodology/approach This study adopts analytical autoethnography grounded in the lead author’s nearly three decades of experience across multinational (MNC) and family-owned organizations in Indonesia, Thailand and New Zealand. Four autobiographical episodes were purposively selected as significant identity-transition events involving digital and sustainability transformation. These episodes were triangulated with public documents and organizational artifacts. Analysis followed three stages: chronological narrative reconstruction, artifact triangulation and iterative interpretation using Identity Theory and Theory of Change (ToC). Findings Identity reconstruction in the Global South unfolded through three recurring mechanisms: (1) translation of Enterprise Resource Planning and big data analytics systems into local practices under asymmetric power relations; (2) reconciliation of global sustainability frameworks with indigenous stewardship values, producing hybrid legitimacy strategies; and (3) adaptive cycles of emotional and political labor as accountants negotiated role conflict across MNC and family-owned contexts. These findings reveal how identity work is structurally conditioned by institutional asymmetry and culturally mediated through relational negotiation, as illustrated by autobiographical episodes. Originality/value This study positions the Global South as a generative context for theorizing identity work under digital and sustainability transformation. It extends identity theory to account for structural asymmetry and cultural negotiation, demonstrates the ToC value for understanding how management accountants construct transformation pathways and advances analytical autoethnography as a rigorous method for revealing the emotional and political dimensions of identity change.

papers.title: Assessing the challenges and lessons learned from the implementation of accrual-based accounting in Indonesian local governments
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to analyze determinants influencing accrual-based accounting implementation in Indonesian Local Governments. This study uses an integrated framework combining Contingency, Organizational Capacity and Institutional Theories to explain implementation variations despite a uniform regulatory environment. Design/methodology/approach This research uses a quantitative approach using secondary data from 214 local government financial reports for the years 2018 and 2019. Regression analysis was conducted to examine the impact of administrative age, regional status (district vs city) and financial independence. The model was rigorously tested and theoretically adjusted to reflect institutional realities, ensuring robust statistical validity. Findings Regional status and financial independence are significant determinants. Cities and regions with higher fiscal autonomy exhibit higher success rates. Conversely, administrative age shows no significant effect, suggesting implementation depends more on current resource capacity than historical experience. The findings of this study regarding the insignificance of age can be interpreted in light of institutional theory, indicating that coercive top-down pressures force standardized compliance regardless of organizational maturity. Practical implications This study highlights that financial autonomy acts as a critical proxy for an organization’s ability to acquire IT infrastructure and skilled human resources. Policymakers should focus on strengthening the fiscal independence of local governments, particularly for district governments (regencies), which lag behind cities in implementation readiness. Originality/value This study empirically demonstrates that under strict regulatory isomorphism, resource capacity outweighs historical factors. This challenges traditional contingency views by showing that organizational maturity offers no comparative advantage in a top-down regulatory environment, bridging the gap between technical adoption and institutionalization.

papers.title: ESG-based pay, corporate sustainability performance and moderating impact of institutions: insights from top global companies
papers.abstract: Purpose The study aims to investigate the association between ESG-based pay and corporate sustainability performance (CSP) and how institutions moderate the relationship. The authors focus on formal (legal system and country institutional quality) and informal (i.e. cultural environment) institutions. Design/methodology/approach Using a panel research design, the authors analyse a sample of the world’s 500 largest companies. Given the panel structure of the data, the authors use firm and year fixed-effects ordinary least squares (OLS) regressions to control for unobserved, time-invariant firm characteristics and common year-specific effects. We further conduct interaction analyses to examine the moderating effects of the variables of interest. To assess the robustness of our findings and address potential differences in observable characteristics between treatment and comparison groups, the authors conduct additional robustness tests using propensity score matching (PSM) and entropy balancing. Findings Results show that ESG-based pay is positively associated with CSP. However, the legal system moderates this relationship, with the positive effect being weaker in common law countries, where firms generally exhibit higher CSP levels. Institutional quality also moderates the relationship, as stronger institutional environments reduce reliance on ESG-linked executive compensation to drive sustainability outcomes. Furthermore, cultural context shapes the effectiveness of ESG-based pay, with some cultural dimensions substituting for and others reinforcing, executive incentive mechanisms. The findings remain robust to alternative sample specifications and tests addressing endogeneity and selection bias. Practical implications The findings offer important practical implications for policymakers and corporate decision-makers. ESG-based executive compensation can be an effective governance mechanism for enhancing CSP. However, its effectiveness depends on the broader institutional and cultural context. Originality/value The authors contribute to knowledge by addressing a gap in the literature on the role of institutions in ESG-based pay and sustainability performance. By exposing the role of formal and informal institutions in shaping the effectiveness of executive compensation packages to achieve sustainability targets, the authors draw attention of stakeholders to the need to consider institutional environments when designing executive compensation packages within the context of CSP.

papers.title: Unraveling performance asymmetry: environmental accounting and knowledge management as economic and environmental decision-support tools in an emerging market
papers.abstract: Purpose This paper aims to examine the asymmetric effect of environmental management accounting (EMA) and environmental knowledge management practices (EKMP) on the financial (FP) and environmental performance (EP) of firms in an emerging market. Design/methodology/approach It adopted the cross-sectional design with stratified random sampling and PLS-SEM to analyze data from 347 respondents across manufacturing firms in Ghana. Findings The findings reveal an important asymmetry in the performance consequences of EMA. While EMA significantly improves FP, it does not exert a corresponding influence on EP, suggesting that EMA functions primarily as an economic decision-support mechanism rather than a direct environmental improvement tool. Conversely, EKMP contributes to FP, but the magnitude of its effect is relatively small and less direct than its influence on EP. Research limitations/implications The complex effect of EKMP on FP suggests that environmental performance may serve as an intermediate mechanism through which EKMP enhances FP; thus, the nexus should be mediated by factors like EP, ESG and green innovation. Practical implications Managers should not treat EMA and EKMP as interchangeable practices. EMA should primarily support financial and managerial control through environmental cost identification, resource allocation, budgeting, investment appraisal and operational decision-making. EKMP, in contrast, should be developed as an organizational capability. Firms must intentionally transition from passive compliance to active eco-innovations and sustainable production technologies fueled by internal EKMP to achieve tangible environmental targets. Originality/value By synthesizing the resource-based view and knowledge-based view theories, this paper provides pioneering evidence that EMA and EKMP govern completely different performance dimensions. The ultimate value of this work is proving that true corporate sustainability cannot be achieved through fragmented, single-framework approaches; instead, firms must structurally integrate financial-accounting controls with cognitive knowledge systems to achieve complete, balanced performance in volatile emerging markets.

papers.title: Bridging the AI divide: local public accountants’ perceptions and structural constraints in AI readiness
papers.abstract: Purpose This research aims to explore whether an emerging “Artificial Intelligence (AI) divide” is developing in local public accounting due to disparities in professional attitudes, financial capacity, technological resources and political governance. Design/methodology/approach A quantitative approach was employed using survey data from 172 Spanish municipalities, combined with real financial and political indicators. A linear regression model with clustered standard errors was applied to test the hypotheses. Findings Findings are consistent with an emerging AI divide in local public accounting in terms of uneven intention to use AI and institutional readiness conditions. Results indicate that public accountants are willing to assume the learning effort required to use AI when clear benefits and a legitimising environment are present. Regarding structural conditions, municipalities with stronger financial sustainability and higher economic development display greater readiness, while advanced technological resources diminish intention, potentially reflecting institutional inertia. In addition, the findings suggest that AI readiness is becoming a cross-cutting priority that depends on governments’ ability to articulate coherent strategies. Originality/value This study provides actionable value for public accountants and governments by clarifying how they can prevent an AI divide from emerging. Public accountants can assess digital readiness, advocate for training and resources and take a strategic role in leading AI-driven innovation. For local governments, it provides guidance on creating enabling conditions for AI adoption through pilots, strategic planning, financial stability and inter-municipal cooperation, while highlighting how higher-level administrations can support cohesion through shared services and capacity-building.

papers.title: Moving beyond the invisible: hidden cost accounting as a mediating device for organizational change in crisis-stricken small family-owned businesses
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how hidden cost calculations produced through the Socio-Economic Approach to Management (SEAM) mediate organizational sensemaking and professionalization in a crisis-stricken small family-owned business. Design/methodology/approach An intervention-research design using the SEAM and its Qualimetrics protocol, based on a longitudinal case study of a Lebanese industrial small family-owned business. Findings Hidden cost calculations made informal dysfunctions visible, discussable and connectable to managerial routines, functioning as mediating accounting representations rather than mechanically triggering change. Post-intervention figures are interpreted as part of the intervention record, not as causal proof of effectiveness. Research limitations/implications As a single intervention-research case, the findings are analytically rather than statistically generalizable. The hidden cost figures are negotiated estimates produced within the intervention and are not read as independent causal measurements of performance improvement. Practical implications For owner-managers, hidden cost accounting may offer a route to professionalization by translating coordination delays, rework, skill gaps and idle time into financial terms, supporting prioritization without immediate bureaucratic expansion. Social implications By making internal sources of loss visible and discussable, hidden cost accounting may help crisis-stricken firms protect productive capacity and shift from reactive cost cutting toward organizational learning. Originality/value The study contributes to interpretive management accounting and organizational change literature by showing how a socio-economic intervention can produce calculative representations through which crisis-stricken small family-owned businesses reinterpret internal dysfunctions and negotiate professionalization.

papers.title: Mapping sustainability reporting using indicator attributes
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how the attributes of reported sustainability indicators can be used to infer the reporting strategies organisations adopt. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on institutional, stakeholder and legitimacy theories, we reviewed the sustainability reporting literature to identify key reporting strategies and related indicator attributes, including reporting frequency, stakeholder focus and the direction and sensitivity of information. These attributes informed a global reporting initiative (GRI)-based coding framework, which we applied to 2,184 GRI-based sustainability reports from 364 US-listed firms in the Forbes Global 2000 between 2018 and 2023. Frequency data were analysed quantitatively, while the remaining attributes were independently coded and mapped to GRI performance indicators. Descriptive trend analysis, comparative distribution analysis and regression models were then used to examine how disclosure profiles differed across reporting groups and evolved over time. The framework was subsequently applied across the sample to identify and compare firms’ reporting strategies. Findings Indicator attributes reveal strategic differences not visible from disclosure counts alone. Firms with similar disclosure volumes may allocate reporting attention very differently across indicators, stakeholders and disclosure types, while firms with differing disclosure volumes may exhibit similar reporting profiles. The findings show that increases in disclosure volume do not necessarily correspond to broader disclosure coverage or more inclusive reporting strategies. Although reporting levels generally increased over time, disclosure profiles changed only modestly, with firms largely maintaining similar reporting orientations across the study period. A firm’s reporting approach may also appear broader under one theoretical lens but selective or concentrated under another, highlighting the importance of using multiple perspectives when assessing sustainability disclosure strategies. Originality/value The study shows the value of examining sustainability reports through multiple theoretical perspectives and introduces a structured, theory-informed approach for analysing reporting content.

papers.journal: Journal of Accounting in Emerging Economies
papers.title: CEO structural power and earnings persistence: the moderating role of organizational complexity
papers.abstract: Purpose This paper investigates the association between CEO structural power and earnings persistence and examines the moderating role of organizational complexity in shaping this relationship. We hypothesize that the association is non-linear and becomes more negative in firms with high organizational complexity. Design/methodology/approach We compile a hand collected dataset covering the full population of publicly traded entities listed on Georgia's capital market, comprising 249 firm year observations over 2018–2023. Our empirical strategy applies pooled first order autoregressions of net income and a three-way interaction model that allows the earnings persistence coefficient to vary with CEO structural power and firm complexity. Findings The findings show that CEO structural power has a stronger negative effect on earnings persistence in complex firms than in less complex firms. In complex firms, separating the CEO and board-chair roles signals enhanced internal control and meets external investors' expectations. In less complex firms, however, high CEO structural power may streamline decision-making and improve earnings persistence. Additional tests reveal that the negative association persists but is substantially weakened when a strong controlling owner is present, suggesting that powerful owners can enforce oversight mechanisms that constrain managerial discretion. Originality/value This study highlights the importance of organizational complexity in shaping the consequences of CEO structural power and provides a more nuanced understanding of how leadership structure influences earnings quality in emerging market settings.

papers.journal: Journal of Accounting in Emerging Economies
papers.title: AAOIFI standards and income smoothing behavior: evidence from Islamic financial institutions in the MENA region
papers.abstract: Purpose Our study investigates whether the adoption of Accounting and Auditing Organization for Islamic Financial Institutions (AAOIFI) accounting and auditing standards influences income smoothing behavior in Islamic Financial Institutions (IFIs) operating in the Middle East and North African (MENA) region. In particular, we examine whether Financial Accounting Standards (FASs) affect earnings behavior differently from International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) and whether institutions jointly applying AAOIFI accounting and auditing standards exhibit different income smoothing behavior from institutions not applying AAOIFI auditing standards. Design/methodology/approach Using a sample of IFIs from 2013–2018, we employ a multi-method approach combining earnings variability, benchmark-beating tests, and a classification of income smoothing into artificial, real, and natural categories. Findings Our results indicate that IFIs applying AAOIFI FASs exhibit a higher likelihood of income smoothing and lower earnings volatility compared to IFRS-adopting institutions. Institutions jointly applying AAOIFI accounting and auditing standards also exhibit a positive association with income smoothing. However, this association is weaker and less robust across alternative specifications than that observed for FASs. Practical implications Our findings indicate that regulators, auditors and Sharia governance bodies should require transparent, comparable disclosure of reserve movements and other stabilization mechanisms. Such disclosure can help investors and investment account holders distinguish sustainable performance from reporting-induced stability. Originality/value This study provides novel cross-country evidence on AAOIFI standards and income smoothing in IFIs. By separately examining FASs and the joint application of AAOIFI accounting and auditing standards, we extend the Islamic finance and emerging-market accounting literature.

papers.journal: Journal of Accounting in Emerging Economies
papers.title: Internal audit quality and earnings management: the roles of competence, independence, and work performance
papers.abstract: Purpose This study examines whether internal audit quality (IAQ) is associated with lower income-increasing discretionary accruals and improved financial reporting quality (FRQ) in an emerging market with uneven regulatory enforcement. Design/methodology/approach Survey-based measures of internal audit (IA) competence, independence and work performance are combined with archival data from non-financial firms listed on the Dhaka Stock Exchange. FRQ is proxied by signed discretionary accruals from the performance-adjusted modified Jones model (Kothari et al., 2005), and interaction models examine variation across reporting-pressure and governance conditions. Given the cross-sectional design, the findings are associational rather than causal. Findings Higher IAQ is associated with lower income-increasing discretionary accruals. Competence is the attribute primarily associated with this relationship, whereas independence and work performance show no separate association once modelled jointly. The association is stronger among loss-making firms but weaker where audit committee independence is high, a pattern consistent with substitution between IA and audit-committee monitoring, though the interaction is only marginally significant. Evidence on audit committee financial expertise is weaker and is treated as suggestive. Practical implications In emerging markets, the findings highlight the importance of IA expertise, certification and training, and suggest that formal structural arrangements alone may be insufficient for reporting quality. Originality/value The study provides emerging-market evidence consistent with IAQ acting as a substantive monitoring mechanism rather than symbolic compliance, with its disciplining association most evident under higher reporting pressure and weaker structural oversight.
