papers.journal: Journal of Accounting in Emerging Economies
papers.title: Copy, paste, and obfuscate? Readability and standardisation in integrated reporting
papers.abstract: Purpose This study examines how readability and textual similarity evolve and interact in integrated reports, investigating whether narrative accessibility and textual standardisation are distinct characteristics or interconnected features of institutionalised reporting practices. Design/methodology/approach A longitudinal panel of 1,393 firm-year observations from South African listed companies over 2015–2024 is analysed. Readability is measured using Flesch Reading Ease, and textual similarity using cosine similarity between consecutive reports. Fixed-effects panel regressions are supplemented by governance-excluded similarity measures, first-difference models, persistence analysis and an alternative readability measure. Findings Readability declines over time, while textual similarity remains high, with no consistent upward trend. Textual similarity is positively associated with readability, indicating that narrative continuity can coexist with greater accessibility. However, this association becomes insignificant when governance-related disclosures are excluded, suggesting that it is concentrated within a highly institutionalised disclosure domain characterised by recurring reporting requirements and stable narrative structures. Additional analyses confirm the persistence of textual similarity and robustness of the main findings. Originality/value This study extends research that has largely examined readability and textual similarity separately by demonstrating that these characteristics are interrelated and that their association depends on the disclosure domain. Greater readability can coexist with substantial textual standardisation, complicating the interpretation of this as an unambiguous indicator of disclosure quality or transparency. The findings highlight the importance of distinguishing narrative accessibility, textual standardisation and substantive informativeness when evaluating corporate disclosure.

papers.journal: Journal of Accounting in Emerging Economies
papers.title: Private sustainability engagement in an emerging economy
papers.abstract: Purpose This study critically examines how private sustainability engagement functions as a form of dialogic accountability when Nordic institutional investors interact with publicly listed companies in a state-dominated emerging economy, challenging the implicit universalism of consensus-seeking engagement models. Design/methodology/approach The study employs qualitative content analysis of Nordic investor engagement reports documenting extended interactions with Egyptian financial and telecommunication companies. Legitimacy theory, neo-institutional theory and dialogic accountability provide an integrated lens for examining information exchange and corporate answerability. Findings Private engagements centre on political connections and human rights risks, with documented response patterns consistent with a prioritisation of political licence to operate over substantive answerability to international investors. The documented engagements record evidential burdens preventing independent verification. The response patterns across both cases constitute dialogic deadlock – a structural ceiling where genuine accountability exchange is foreclosed. Originality/value Empirically, the study provides an in-depth qualitative content analysis of investor-side engagement reports, documenting the sustainability information Nordic investors seek in two Egyptian private engagements and the patterns of corporate response. Theoretically, it proposes political licence and audience primacy as concepts for interpreting the documented exchanges and specifies the contextual conditions under which audience hierarchy may shift toward audience primacy. Conceptually, it theorises dialogic deadlock as a structural outcome arising where legitimacy incentives prove insufficient and the preconditions for genuine dialogic accountability are constitutively absent.

papers.journal: Journal of Accounting in Emerging Economies
papers.title: Do Big4 accounting firms affect foreign individuals’ investment decisions? Evidence from an emerging market
papers.abstract: Purpose This paper focuses on an emerging market and investigates whether a firm’s audit engagement with a Big4 accounting firm is associated with foreign individuals’ investments. We hypothesize that Big4 accounting firms’ reputation may function as a heuristic trust signal for these investors. Design/methodology/approach We tested our hypothesis by utilizing 225 non-financial firms listed on Borsa Istanbul. The dataset covers 2005 to 2023 and contains 3,590 firm-year observations. Findings Our empirical evidence indicates that foreign individuals are more likely to invest in BIST-listed firms audited by a Big4 accounting firm (AF). Our results are consistent with prior studies showing that accounting firms’ reputation is associated with investors’ decisions. Our robustness analysis suggests that Big4 AFs’ reputation may lose importance when public governance declines. Research limitations/implications The primary limitation of this research is that investor-level data are not publicly available. We also did not incorporate audit-firm-level variables such as expertise and number of partners. Practical implications Our study has implications for managers, policymakers and accounting professionals. Managers seeking to signal trust to foreign individuals may consider the positive association between Big4 AF engagement and foreign investment. Social implications Policymakers should consider measures to enhance public governance quality to attract more foreign individuals to Borsa Istanbul. Big4 AFs should note that this reputational advantage weakens as public governance declines. Originality/value While prior studies have examined institutional investors’ and mutual funds’ preferences for Big4 accounting firms, this study contributes new archival evidence on foreign individual investors’ equity investment decisions in relation to Big4 engagement in an emerging market context.

papers.journal: Journal of Accounting in Emerging Economies
papers.title: Auditors' experiences of the impact of ISA 701 on audit practice and audit accountability in South African state-owned enterprises
papers.abstract: Purpose This study explores how public sector auditors experience and interprets the implementation of International Standard on Auditing (ISA) 701, which mandates the communication of key audit matters (KAMs), with particular attention to its perceived implications for audit practice and accountability in the audit of South African State-Owned Enterprises (SOE). Design/methodology/approach The sample comprises senior external auditors and technical managers with expertise in SOE auditing in South Africa. A qualitative phenomenological approach was employed, utilising semi-structured interviews. Findings The findings suggest that auditors experienced changes in several aspects of audit practice following the implementation of ISA 701. Participants described increased technical training focused on identifying and responding to client-specific risks, as well as more structured engagement between audit leaders and audit teams in discussions of significant risks. The implementation of ISA 701 was also associated with greater involvement of technical staff, a strengthened audit review process, and an increased emphasis on professional judgement. While these changes were most evident in documentation and review practices, participants reported more limited shifts in the underlying audit approach over time as KAMs became more routine. The practice of benchmarking risk and audit procedure documentation was identified as a barrier to a client-specific, risk-based audit approach, which some participants viewed as limiting its broader implications for public accountability. Originality/value This study contributes to the literature on the application of new international auditing standards by public sector auditors and offers insight into how such standards are operationalised and mobilised to influence auditors' behaviour.

papers.journal: Journal of Accounting in Emerging Economies
papers.title: The influence pathway of internal audit attributes on credit risk management in emerging economies: evidence from Tanzania
papers.abstract: Purpose This study investigates how internal audit function (IAF) attributes, namely competence, independence, and leadership, influence credit risk management (CRM) in Tanzanian commercial banks, focussing on the mediating role of the IAF's sphere of influence. Design/methodology/approach Data were collected from 131 relevant employees across all 34 licenced commercial banks in Tanzania. A cross-sectional survey design was applied, and partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) was used to test direct and mediated relationships. Findings Results show that IAF competence and independence significantly enhance CRM both directly and indirectly through the sphere of influence, while the relationship between leadership and CRM is fully mediated by the sphere of influence. Moreover, the sphere of influence exerts a significant positive effect on CRM, underscoring the importance of organisational influence in translating audit insights into effective risk governance. Practical implications The findings suggest that banks in emerging economies should reinforce auditor independence and competence while fostering organisational cultures that empower internal audit functions. Regulators are also encouraged to refine their supervisory frameworks to emphasise the institutional role of internal audits in risk oversight. Originality/value This study extends internal auditing research by conceptualising and validating the sphere of influence as the mechanism through which IAF attributes affect CRM. By integrating Agency Theory and Role Theory into a unified capacity–conversion framework, in which audit attributes create monitoring capacity and organisational influence converts it into governance outcomes, it offers new evidence from an emerging economy and advances understanding of how internal audit creates governance value through risk oversight in developing banking systems.

papers.title: Overcoming information asymmetries through non-financial statement assurance: empirical evidence from German listed firms
papers.abstract: Purpose Ongoing discussions about the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) under the Omnibus Initiative question whether the benefits of non-financial reporting and assurance justify their costs. Consequently, this study examines whether assurance of non-financial statements is associated with lower perceived information asymmetry in capital markets. Design/methodology/approach Using hand-collected assurance data for German listed firms (DAX) from 2019 to 2022 under the Non-Financial Reporting Directive (NFRD), we examine associations between voluntary assurance and (1) bid–ask spreads (capital-market information asymmetry) and (2) dispersion across major environmental, social and governance (ESG) ratings (intermediary disagreement). Findings Voluntary assurance is associated with narrower bid–ask spreads, consistent with lower perceived information asymmetry. This relation is not moderated by the assurance level or by having the same engagement partner sign both the financial and non-financial audit opinion. Assurance is also linked to lower ESG rating dispersion, but rating dispersion itself is unrelated to bid–ask spreads. Research limitations/implications Evidence is from the German institutional setting with voluntary assurance; potential self-selection bias limits causal claims. The novel hand-collected dataset extends NFRD assurance research and enables future cross-country work on assurance design. Practical implications Assurance is associated with lower investor information frictions and greater consistency across ESG ratings, supporting the usefulness of non-financial assurance for capital-market participants. The information-asymmetry-reducing effect of assurance appears to operate directly, rather than through ESG ratings, informing standard-setting and the CSRD cost–benefit debate. Originality/value Combining market-based and rating-based proxies in a continental European, civil-law setting with supervisory-board monitoring, we provide evidence that assurance can support the CSRD objective of more credible ESG disclosure.

papers.title: The emerging role of artificial intelligence in financial and management accounting: insights from a systematic literature review and bibliometric analysis
papers.abstract: Purpose This study addresses the fragmentation of research on artificial intelligence (AI) in financial and management accounting through a bibliometric examination of the literature, at a time when AI is reshaping reporting timeliness, audit quality, fraud detection and managerial decision-making while raising governance and explainability risks that current disclosure and assurance frameworks were not designed to address. Design/methodology/approach The study employs a systematic literature review combined with bibliometric analysis, drawing on 245 peer-reviewed articles indexed in the Scopus database over the period 1985–2026. Following PRISMA guidelines, performance analysis and science-mapping techniques are applied using Biblioshiny and VOSviewer. Findings The keyword co-occurrence analysis identifies six thematic clusters: AI as a methodological umbrella; core enablers like machine learning and big data; AI-enabled financial decision support for small and medium-sized enterprises; advanced analytics in finance and forecasting; AI-enabled risk and organisational forecasting; and technical foundations of AI-driven risk assessment. The bibliographic coupling identifies six document clusters spanning fraud detection, neural network applications, management accounting, digital transformation, financial distress/credit risk and AI ethics/governance. Machine learning, financial management and risk assessment are basic themes near the motor-theme boundary, while financial accounting sits in the emerging/declining quadrant. The field moves from expert systems (1985–2010) through machine learning/analytics (2011–2020) to AI governance and ethical accountability (2021–2026). Research limitations/implications The analysis is restricted to Scopus-indexed, peer-reviewed journal articles, excluding Web of Science, conference proceedings and practitioner reports. As a bibliometric study, the methods identify structural patterns and intellectual trends but cannot assess causal mechanisms, qualitative depth or implementation-level outcomes, and the post-2023 rise of generative AI means the snapshot will need periodic updating. Future research should employ empirical, longitudinal and mixed-methods designs to examine the organisational, contextual and ethical implications of AI adoption across diverse accounting environments and regulatory settings. Practical implications These findings are relevant for accounting professionals, managers, auditors, educators and regulators involved in both internal management processes and external financial reporting. By systematically mapping the evolution and thematic structure of AI in financial and management accounting, the study shows how AI tools enhance reporting timeliness, analytical depth and decision usefulness while raising concerns related to transparency, explainability and governance. The results can support accounting educators in curriculum redesign, assist practitioners in aligning AI adoption with reporting objectives and inform regulators in revisiting disclosure requirements, assurance frameworks and internal controls. Originality/value The study examines AI jointly across financial and management accounting, extends coverage to 2026 and proposes a governance-anchored three-layer framework grounded in the resource-based view and socio-technical systems theory.

papers.title: Do auditors price goodwill impairments? The role of audit committee accounting expertise
papers.abstract: Purpose This study examines the association between goodwill impairments, under International Accounting Standard (IAS) 36, and audit fees in the French setting and tests whether audit committee accounting expertise moderates this relationship. Design/methodology/approach Based on a sample of 1,926 firm-year observations from 214 French publicly listed firms over the period 2011–2019, this study estimates panel regressions with firm and year fixed effects and panel-corrected standard errors, complemented by several robustness analyses. Findings The results show that goodwill impairments are positively associated with audit fees and that this association is stronger when impairment losses are larger. The interaction with the binary measure of audit committee accounting expertise is negative and marginally significant, while the continuous measure of expertise provides stronger evidence of a weaker audit fee premium. Research limitations/implications This study relies on archival data and cannot directly observe the coordination process between joint auditors; the coordination-based interpretation of the observed fee premium therefore remains indirect. Future research using more granular audit process data could provide stronger evidence on how joint auditors coordinate the assessment of highly judgmental accounting estimates such as goodwill impairment. Practical implications The findings suggest that goodwill impairments under IAS 36 are associated with higher audit fees in a joint-audit environment. For boards and audit committees, appointing members with accounting expertise may reduce ambiguity over impairment assumptions and help contain the fee premium linked to complex valuation judgments. For regulators and standard setters, the evidence indicates that the costs of the impairment-only model may extend beyond financial statement preparers and are also reflected in audit pricing, particularly in institutional settings where auditors must align their assessments of subjective estimates before issuing a joint opinion. Originality/value This study extends evidence on goodwill impairment pricing to the French mandatory joint-audit setting and documents that audit committee accounting expertise is associated with variation in the audit fee premium. The findings also provide indirect evidence consistent with coordination considerations across auditor-pair configurations in joint audits.

papers.title: Gender and respect in leadership: voices from ExCo women in the financial sector
papers.abstract: Purpose The purpose of this article is to explore the role gender plays in the respect accorded to women leaders in the financial sector. Furthermore, the article seeks to identify ways in which disrespect is related to systemic legitimacy deficits experienced by women leaders in the sector. Design/methodology/approach This study uses a qualitative research design. Fieldwork gathered data through twenty in-depth semi-structured interviews with senior women leaders in a range of financial sector organisations. Fifteen interviews were conducted with UK leaders with remaining interviews conducted with leaders in the United States, Belgium, Brazil and The Channel Islands. Findings In a sector historically constructed as masculine terrain, findings show that women leaders in finance experience gender based (dis)respect, both overt and systemic, in ways that are related to conditional and contingent legitimacy. Women in senior leader positions are often positioned as “space invaders” to the sector. Strategic interrogation of respect and legitimacy cultures can be initiated through a systems approach. Originality/value This study frames the under-researched issue of gendered respect in leadership as a consequential construct, substantively linked to leadership legitimacy. It suggests that the notion of respect can be leveraged and embedded in the systems, structures and shared values of an organisation and can become a valuable vehicle to advance inclusion.

papers.journal: Journal of Public Budgeting, Accounting and Financial Management
papers.title: From disclosure to fiscal discipline: how accounting standards shape public pension plan management
papers.abstract: Purpose Financial reporting transparency is central to effective public-sector governance, yet its impact on managerial decisions in the public sector is understudied. This study examines the extent to which changes in accounting standards are associated with the accounting and management practices of public pension plans. Design/methodology/approach The study employs quantitative analysis of panel data from 181 US public pension plans from 2009 to 2019 before and after the issuance of Governmental Accounting Standards Board Statements No. 67 and 68. Findings The findings show that after the implementation of accounting standards changes, there is a decreasing trend in discount rates and a corresponding increase in reported pension liabilities. More importantly, this enhanced transparency is associated with an increase in employer contributions and more conservative investment return assumptions. Practical implications The findings suggest that policymakers and regulators can use accounting standards as a lever to improve financial management. Consistent recognition and disclosure of liabilities are essential to strengthening fiscal discipline and preventing the obscuring of funding shortfalls. Originality/value This study provides empirical evidence of the link between accounting transparency and managerial decisions in the public sector. It demonstrates that transparency does not merely change how numbers look on a balance sheet; it can influence the decision-making processes regarding contributions and investment risk, particularly in fiscally distressed environments.

papers.journal: Journal of Public Budgeting, Accounting and Financial Management
papers.title: Framing sustainability: the role of municipal enterprises in municipal political discourse
papers.abstract: Purpose This study investigates how municipally owned enterprises (MOEs) are discursively mobilised within city council deliberations on sustainability and how this mobilisation contributes to the construction of public value and legitimacy. Design/methodology/approach The study adopts an interpretive qualitative approach based on abductive qualitative content analysis of 90 municipal council minutes produced between 2021 and 2024 in an Italian municipality. Findings The analysis identifies three complementary modes of mobilisation – strategic, symbolic and hybrid – through which councillors' position MOEs differently depending on the governance issues under discussion. The findings show that these modes are context-dependent rather than fixed organisational characteristics. They also reveal an uneven local public value circuit: community concerns are translated through political deliberation into organisational expectations, whereas sustainability reporting provides only limited feedback into political scrutiny and decision-making. Research limitations/implications The findings suggest that sustainability governance in MOEs should be understood not only through managerial or reporting practices but also through the political processes that shape organisational roles and responsibilities. Although grounded in a single Italian municipal context, the study provides analytically relevant insights into the discursive construction of MOEs within local governance. Originality/value The study extends research on hybrid public organisations by shifting attention from hybridity as an organisational condition to the political processes that make different dimensions of hybridity salient. It introduces discursive mobilisation as a mechanism through which MOE governance roles are constructed within political deliberation and refines the local public value circuit by identifying an incomplete feedback loop between sustainability reporting and municipal political debate.

papers.journal: Journal of Public Budgeting, Accounting and Financial Management
papers.title: The changing role of commonwealth CFOs: reflections from the Allan Barton memorial lecture and implications for public sector accounting
papers.abstract: Purpose This paper examines the challenges facing commonwealth chief financial officers (CFOs), drawing on insights from Stephen Groves' 2026 Allan Barton memorial lecture and observations from auditor-general reports. It argues that CFOs are becoming less strategic because budgeting remains focused on cash, accrual accounting is underused, and financial statements receive limited parliamentary attention. The paper considers the implications for public sector accounting education and research. Design/methodology/approach The paper draws on the Allan Barton memorial lecture, supported by auditor-general reports and professional experience in public sector accounting. Using a practical and interpretive approach, it examines issues including budgeting, depreciation, lease accounting and the limited use of accrual accounting in government decision making. Findings The lecture highlighted how commonwealth CFOs are increasingly focused on compliance and short-term cash management rather than strategic financial leadership. Accrual accounting plays a limited role in budgeting, depreciation is not well integrated into planning, and lease accounting remains difficult to apply. Materiality concepts can also result in issues involving very large sums being treated as immaterial. These issues demonstrate a disconnect between reporting, budgeting and long-term financial management across government. Research limitations/implications The paper is based on one public lecture, selected auditor-general reports and professional experience. While the observations may not reflect every commonwealth agency, they raise broader questions about financial capability, budgeting and reporting practices across government and identify opportunities for further research. Practical implications The paper identifies opportunities to strengthen the strategic role of CFOs through greater use of accrual accounting in budgeting, capital planning and decision making. It points to the need for clearer reporting and better use of balance sheet information to support long-term financial management. Social implications Better financial management can support stronger accountability, more informed decision making and greater public confidence in government. Originality/value The paper provides a practice-based perspective on the challenges facing commonwealth CFOs, based on the lived experience of a senior public sector CFO. It highlights issues that are widely recognised within government but receive limited attention in academic literature, including the weak connection between budgeting and reporting, the growing compliance burden on CFOs and the limited use of accrual accounting.

papers.journal: Journal of Public Budgeting, Accounting and Financial Management
papers.title: Toward resilient inter-organizational collaboration through boundary work: the perspective of frontline managers
papers.abstract: Purpose Public service organizations increasingly rely on inter-organizational collaboration to address complex societal problems that no single actor can manage alone. Public sector managers are representative for initiating and sustaining such collaboration. However, resilient inter-organizational collaboration is proven to be challenging in practice due to various forms of boundaries while previous research largely overlooks managerial boundary work from a processual view. This paper aims to enhance the understanding of developing resilient inter-organizational collaboration in public service organizations from the perspective of frontline managers who are directly involved in collaborative efforts across boundaries. Design/methodology/approach In this longitudinal qualitative single case study, we draw on participant observations of meetings and semi-structured interviews with frontline managers who represent five different caregivers in a new multi-disciplinary primary care model in a Swedish region. Our thematical analysis builds on 24 observed meetings and 10 interviews. Findings The findings show how the studied managers engage in three forms of collaborative boundary work in correspondence to three recurring boundaries in relation to administration, time and communication. The managers employ boundary work strategies in the form of managerial tactics to create a “third space”, embrace a complementary, proactive and accepting approach, and create a new “shared domain”. The tactics help to transform points of friction into points of connection and, ultimately, support the development of resilient inter-organizational collaboration. The paper contributes to research on inter-organizational collaboration by offering a processual understanding of how resilience actively unfolds through five managerial tactics in early stages of work to address common boundaries in relation to administration, time and communication. Secondly, it extends research on collaborative boundary work by illustrating how collaboration is developed through a trilogy of practices for the direct purpose of fostering collaboration in a situated inter-organizational setting with multiple boundaries and actors. Thirdly, it adds an important nuance to this theory by highlighting that collaborative boundary work practices are not inherently stable mechanisms but rather contingent upon the persistence of social conditions. Originality/value Whereas prior research often focuses on collaboration from a predominant instrumental perspective, this paper illustrates it as an unfolding process between individuals and demonstrates how resilient inter-organizational collaboration is possible to reach early on. The paper offers a novel angle on managerial boundary work in direct relation to collaboration.

papers.journal: Journal of Public Budgeting, Accounting and Financial Management
papers.title: Climate reporting in public sector organisations: identity construction and changes
papers.abstract: Purpose The purpose of this article is to explore climate change reporting by public sector organisations. In particular, the analysis draws attention to how public sector organisations represent themselves through climate reporting practice to construct and reproduce their identities over time. Design/methodology/approach A comprehensive content analysis of 164 annual and stand-alone sustainability reports produced by 15 public sector organisations listed on the Australian National Greenhouse and Energy Reporting register over an 11-year period from 2014 to 2024 was used for this study. The analysis is informed by Tregidga et al.'s (2014) identity framework of sustainable organisations. Findings The analysis reveals an unbalanced pattern of identity construction in public sector climate reporting, characterised by a strong focus on compliance-oriented reporting, followed by reporting on climate leadership and limited engagement with strategically “good” practices associated with legitimacy seeking. Despite evidence of more substantive climate reporting, disclosures continue to focus predominantly on metrics and statistics reflecting regulatory and policy expectations. The longitudinal analysis reinforces this identity structure, although their climate reporting has developed into a more complex communicative space through which public sector organisations simultaneously construct multiple identities over time, implying that public sector climate reporting serves as a dynamic and ongoing process of identity construction rather than a linear transition from one identity to another. The analysis across organisational types also reveals that a compliance-oriented identity is most pronounced among local governments and moderately prominent in public service organisations, whereas a leadership-oriented identity emphasising community impact and knowledge sharing is most strongly developed in public universities. Originality/value Despite the rapid development of climate reporting in corporate contexts, research on sustainability and climate reporting in the public sector is still underdeveloped, even as these organisations increasingly recognise the importance of disclosing, governing and managing climate-related impacts. This article fills the gap by exploring how disclosures on climate change have evolved over time within public sector organisations to contribute to accountability and effective policy implementation. It extends Tregidga et al.'s (2014) organisational identity framework to a public sector context, where climate reporting is characterised by the coexistence of regulatory, public value and legitimacy considerations.

papers.journal: Sustainability Accounting, Management and Policy Journal
papers.title: Climate policy uncertainty and corporate boilerplate information disclosure strategies: a perspective on attention-based view
papers.abstract: Purpose Facing climate policy uncertainty, firms may adjust their information disclosure strategies in response to external pressures. This not only may conceal substantive transformation information but also may lead to capital misallocation, thereby hindering the process of the low-carbon transition. Drawing on the attention-based view, this paper aims to examine how climate policy uncertainty influences corporate disclosure strategies. Design/methodology/approach Using a sample of Chinese A-share listed companies from 2008 to 2022, this paper empirically examines the impact of climate policy uncertainty on firms’ boilerplate disclosure of climate transition information. Findings The results indicate that heightened climate policy uncertainty significantly increases the extent of boilerplate disclosure. Mechanism analysis reveals two primary channels: curbing substantive environmental investments and reinforcing managerial risk aversion. Furthermore, moderating tests show that organizational inertia exacerbates the effect, whereas corporate digitalization and CEOs’ political background effectively mitigate it. Practical implications The findings suggest that policymakers should establish stable, long-term policy frameworks with specific and verifiable disclosure guidelines to steer firms away from symbolic compliance toward genuine green transformation. Social implications This study shifts sustainable governance analysis from substantive production to strategic information communication, emphasizing the need for policy coherence and regulatory credibility in fostering transparent climate communication, thereby optimizing climate governance for global stakeholders and providing a reference for directing capital toward truly sustainable development projects. Originality/value This paper extends the attention-based view to corporate sustainability communication, innovatively identifying boilerplate disclosure as an overlooked impediment to sustainability progress and enriching the literature on climate policy uncertainty from an information disclosure perspective.

papers.journal: Sustainability Accounting, Management and Policy Journal
papers.title: Setting corporate sustainability targets: a qualitative analysis of sustainability reporting in the automotive industry
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine a sample of companies in the automotive industry over a ten-year period to analyze their target-setting approaches and efforts to achieve legitimacy by disclosing corporate sustainability targets. Design/methodology/approach Using a qualitative approach, the authors conduct a content analysis of sustainability reporting to explore the evolution of the publication of corporate sustainability targets. The authors analyze disclosures of corporate sustainability targets in sustainability, annual and integrated reports from six automotive companies from 2012 to 2022. Findings The results demonstrate considerable variation and inconsistency in the reporting of corporate sustainability targets over time. The authors identify distinct target attributes that demonstrate symbolic or substantive approaches to legitimacy. Practical implications The findings support ongoing developments in standard-setting practices, particularly regarding the specification of target-related disclosure attributes associated with substantive legitimacy. The study’s findings also assist investors and other stakeholders in assessing the commitment of the companies that disclose corporate sustainability targets. Social implications By examining sustainability targets that reflect both substantive and symbolic legitimization approaches, this study shows how companies set and report these targets in practice. This study enables stakeholders to better assess the credibility of corporate sustainability commitments, thereby enhancing transparency and accountability and supporting progress toward sustainable development and the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals. Originality/value The authors’ focus on the automotive industry provides insight into an industry under high stakeholder and especially regulatory pressure. Combined with their in-depth qualitative analysis of reporting on corporate sustainability targets, the authors provide new insights into forward-looking sustainability disclosure.

papers.journal: Sustainability Accounting, Management and Policy Journal
papers.title: The evolution of legitimacy discourse in corporate social responsibility reporting: evidence from a state-owned Irish energy company (2003-2025)
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how legitimacy is discursively constructed and stabilised over time in corporate social responsibility (CSR) reporting in a state-owned enterprise (SOE) and what these legitimacy dynamics reveal about how an SOE responds to evolving sustainable-development expectations. Design/methodology/approach The CSR sections of the Electricity Supply Board’s annual reports from 2003 to 2025 are analysed using a theory-informed computerised content analysis based on Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count categories mapped to Suchman’s (1995) legitimacy framework. To assess the mapping’s interpretive validity, the authors incorporate several robustness analyses. Findings Over the 23-year period studied, the reports increasingly and consistently used language that conveyed a sense of the ESB as a natural, accepted part of everyday life. While the report language reflected pragmatic and moral legitimacy, cognitive legitimacy was prominent. This prominence is observed across multiple analytical approaches, suggesting a stable discursive orientation. This finding suggests that in SOE contexts, legitimacy depends less on actively persuading stakeholders and more on being perceived as taken-for-granted in society. Sustainable-development transitions occur through organisations whose historically embedded societal roles can both support continuity and require continuing accountability as sustainable-development expectations change. Research limitations/implications The study focuses on a single case. Also, the operationalisation of legitimacy through linguistic proxies involves interpretive judgement. While robustness checks provide support for the findings, the results should be understood as indicative patterns, not precise measurements. Practical implications The findings highlight CSR reporting as a component of managing long-term legitimacy, particularly for publicly accountable organisations. Managers may draw on historically embedded narratives and societal connections to enhance trust and alignment with sustainable-development expectations. Social implications For policymakers and regulators, the findings suggest that sustainability reporting is more than a compliance exercise – it is part of a wider infrastructure supporting public accountability and long-term societal value, and this should inform how reporting is designed. For organisations, actively cultivating a sense of being a trusted part of society through reporting can strengthen stakeholder ties and support broader sustainable development efforts. Originality/value This study provides longitudinal evidence on the configuration of legitimacy forms in CSR reporting, showing that legitimacy dynamics in SOEs differ from prior literature and the relevance of historically accumulated legitimacy to sustainable development. It also contributes methodologically by proxying legitimacy types to automated text analysis.

papers.journal: Sustainability Accounting, Management and Policy Journal
papers.title: Unveiling ESG ratings: corporate perspectives and institutionalisation dynamics
papers.abstract: Purpose Environmental, social and governance (ESG) ratings have become a central mechanism for assessing, benchmarking and signalling corporate sustainability performance to financial investors. Yet, their widespread use persists despite ongoing criticism of their capacity to accurately reflect firms’ social and environmental contributions. This paper aims to examine this paradox from the perspective of rated companies, exploring why firms continue to engage with ESG ratings despite criticism of their effectiveness, even as investors remain their primary users. Drawing on institutional theory, the authors adopt this underexplored perspective and investigate how ESG ratings become institutionalised within organisations. Design/methodology/approach Based on abductive thematic analysis of 45 semi-structured interviews with sustainability executives from listed European firms, the authors develop a framework distinguishing between substantive and symbolic forms of ESG rating institutionalisation. Findings ESG rating adoption is shaped by institutional pressures and unfolds along a continuum. At one end, firms substantively integrate sustainability considerations into core operations; at the other, ESG ratings are used symbolically to secure external recognition and legitimacy. This study also highlights the risk of deinstitutionalisation if the limitations of ESG ratings remain unaddressed. Practical implications This study offers managers, investors and policymakers insights into navigating ESG pressures and strengthening the credibility of ESG frameworks while providing a diagnostic lens to distinguish symbolic compliance from substantive integration. Social implications While the potential deinstitutionalisation of ESG ratings could erode credibility, accountability and investor trust, substantive adoption could benefit transparency, stakeholder oversight and the diffusion of sustainability norms. Addressing their limitations is therefore crucial for maintaining credibility in the financial sector and directing capital towards companies with meaningful sustainability practices. Originality/value This study extends research on corporate responses to ESG ratings by drawing on institutional theory and developing a conceptual framework of symbolic and substantive institutionalisation from the perspective of rated companies. Specifically, it shifts the explanatory focus beyond firms’ strategic orientations by showing that corporate responses are also shaped by the institutional characteristics and structural limitations of ESG rating systems, thereby advancing the concept of ESG ratings’ deinstitutionalisation.

papers.journal: Sustainability Accounting, Management and Policy Journal
papers.title: Board monitoring and the informational content of ESG performance
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine whether improvements in environmental, social and governance (ESG) performance are associated with subsequent realised firm outcomes and whether board monitoring conditions these relationships. Using UK FTSE 350 firms, the study evaluates whether year-on-year ESG improvements predict ESG controversies, environmental incidents, investment inefficiency and future operating performance. It further investigates whether stronger board monitoring increases the extent to which ESG improvements are associated with favourable subsequent outcomes. Design/methodology/approach The study uses an unbalanced panel of 314 FTSE 350 firms, comprising 4,396 firm-year observations from 2010 to 2024, with ESG, governance and financial data from LSEG. Panel regressions include industry and year fixed effects with firm-clustered standard errors. Board monitoring is measured using a composite index based on board independence, CEO-chair role separation and board ESG expertise. Robustness tests include disaggregated governance components, an ESG measure excluding the governance pillar, firm fixed effects, lagged specifications and multicollinearity diagnostics. Findings ESG improvements are not consistently associated with subsequent ESG controversies, investment inefficiency or future operating performance. For environmental incidents, however, the interaction between ESG improvement and board monitoring is negative and statistically significant, indicating that the association becomes more favourable as monitoring strengthens. Component-level analyses show similar negative moderation for board independence, CEO-chair separation and ESG expertise, although statistical strength varies. The result also remains when the governance pillar is excluded from the ESG measure. Lagged specifications provide more limited evidence, indicating that the relationship is outcome-specific and not persistent across all time horizons. Research limitations/implications The study focuses on UK listed firms operating within a relatively strong governance environment, which may limit generalisability to weaker institutional settings. The board monitoring index uses equal weighting, although component-level tests reduce concerns regarding this construction. The outcome measures capture specific dimensions of realised firm behaviour and do not directly measure greenwashing, managerial intent or board detection processes. Future research could examine alternative governance measures, weighting schemes, outcome intensity, other institutional settings and additional mechanisms such as ownership structure, executive incentives and external assurance. Practical implications The findings suggest that ESG score improvements should not be interpreted in isolation as evidence of substantive operational change. For boards, the results highlight the importance of effective oversight in linking ESG initiatives to underlying business practices, particularly in environmentally sensitive areas. For investors, ESG changes may be more informative when considered alongside governance characteristics. For regulators and standard setters, the evidence suggests that enhanced ESG disclosure alone may be insufficient unless supported by governance structures that promote accountability and substantive implementation. Social implications The study has broader implications for corporate accountability and stakeholder confidence in ESG information. By showing that ESG improvements are not uniformly associated with realised outcomes, the findings reinforce the need for stronger governance and scrutiny over how sustainability claims relate to actual corporate behaviour. More credible alignment between ESG performance and operational conduct may improve the usefulness of sustainability information for employees, communities, investors and other stakeholders and may help reduce the risk that symbolic improvements are interpreted as evidence of substantive social or environmental progress. Originality/value The study contributes by shifting attention from ESG levels to the informational content of ESG improvements and their association with subsequent realised outcomes. It further shows that this relationship is conditional on board monitoring and differs across outcome types. Unlike studies focused mainly on ESG disclosure or contemporaneous firm value, this study links changes in ESG performance to future adverse events, investment efficiency and operating performance. It also provides new evidence that the environmental-outcome relationship is not solely driven by the construction of the composite monitoring index or mechanical overlap with the ESG governance pillar.

papers.title: Presidential Address: Human Finance: Incorporating Insights from the Life Sciences
papers.abstract: Many of the key determinants of human behavior identified in the life sciences, such as stress response, impulse control, and mood regulation, remain absent from standard economic and finance models. This paper illustrates how such insights can enhance economic models in the context of inflation expectations. Combining a retrospective survey that elicits personal inflation histories with an experimental intervention that induces the reexperiencing of historic inflation, I show that physiological, emotional, and cognitive stress markers predict heightened inflation expectations and sharper memory recall, while also shaping personal economic narratives. These findings suggest novel policy tools to counter the persistent scars of economic distress and crisis experiences, for example, by designing experiences to provide predictability and control.

papers.title: Is Informed Short Selling Concentrated in Family Firms? Evidence from a Reinvestigation
papers.abstract: We reinvestigate Anderson, Reeb, and Zhao's findings that informed short selling is unique to family firms and driven by information leakage from internal disputes. Using the same firm sample and more comprehensive short‐selling data, we find that short selling predicts future returns in both family and nonfamily firms. We also find no significant difference in abnormal short selling before negative earnings announcements. In extended sample periods, short selling continues to predict returns for nonfamily firms under both ownership‐based and familial‐link definitions. Overall, our evidence suggests that short sellers are broadly informed and that family firms are not uniquely vulnerable.

papers.title: Unintended Consequences of Holding Dollar Assets
papers.abstract: We propose and examine a novel mechanism whereby holdings of dollar assets by foreign institutions can have a large, unexpected impact on foreign Treasury yields in crisis periods. Non‐U.S. institutions hold substantial dollar assets and hedge dollar exposures by selling dollars forward. In crisis periods, the dollar appreciates against other currencies. To meet margin calls on foreign exchange (FX) hedging positions, traditionally passive institutions liquidate domestic safe assets to raise cash. We show that during the recent COVID crisis, U.K. institutions with substantial dollar holdings and FX hedging positions sold large amounts of gilts, contributing significantly to the observed gilt yield spike.

papers.title: The Evolution of the Market for Corporate Control
papers.abstract: We consider an informed large shareholder who can choose between making a takeover bid herself and initiating a sale to another acquirer. Such takeover activism complements direct takeovers because the very choice mitigates the asymmetric information problem, thereby improving efficiency. As more investors enter the market for corporate control, takeover activism increasingly replaces direct takeovers as the prevailing mode of disciplinary control change, matching the evolution in practice. Our model shows how this evolution, characterized by a symbiotic relationship between investor activism and private equity, arises to overcome asymmetric information and collective action problems through intermediated transactions.

papers.title: Do Experimental Asset Market Results Replicate? High‐Powered Preregistered Replications of 17 Key Results
papers.abstract: Experimental asset markets provide a controlled approach to studying financial markets. We attempt to replicate 17 key results from four prominent studies, collecting new data from 166 markets with 1,544 participants. Only three of the 14 original results reported as statistically significant were successfully replicated. We fail to replicate findings on emotions, self‐control, and gender differences in bubble formation but confirm that experience reduces bubbles and cognitive skills explain trading success. Our study demonstrates the importance of replications in enhancing the credibility of scientific results in this field.

Fintech Expansion
papers.abstract: I study credit market outcomes with different competing lending technologies: a fintech lender that learns from data and can seize on-platform sales, and a banking sector that relies on physical collateral. Despite flexible information acquisition technology, endogenous fintech learning is surprisingly coarse, with a single threshold that screens out low-quality borrowers. As fintech lending technology improves, better enforcement harms, while better information technology benefits traditional banking sector profits. Big data technology enables the fintech to leverage data from its early-stage operations in unbanked markets to develop predictive models that support expansion into wealthier markets. (JEL G21, L13, L52, O33, O36)

papers.title: Collateral Demand in Wholesale Funding Markets
papers.abstract: Repo markets are systemically important funding markets, but are also used by firms to obtain the assets provided as collateral. We build and structurally estimate a model of trade between heterogeneous firms in the sterling gilt repo market, and show that this collateral demand depresses repo market activity and can impede the transmission of monetary policy. We quantify how well-designed central bank repo facilities can improve outcomes: if the central bank were to lend out the assets on its balance sheet following quantitative easing, transmission and total firm surplus would improve by 20% and 38%, respectively.

papers.title: CHILE
papers.abstract: We introduce CHILE, an asset-pricing framework with asymmetric information, general utility functions, and arbitrary payoffs. It features a large economy (LE) with continuous-and-heterogeneous information (CHI). The defining feature of this information structure is that the total amount of information stays finite as the economy grows large. We use the framework to study how concentration—the presence of market participants of different sizes—affects market quality, namely liquidity and information efficiency. Greater concentration proves a double-edged sword: it raises liquidity but harms information efficiency. (JEL D01, D53, D82, E19, G12, G14)

papers.title: Climate Risk Disclosure and Risk Sharing in Financial Markets
papers.abstract: In this paper, I model how climate risk disclosure impacts climate risk sharing among investors. I show that this disclosure can improve risk sharing by helping investors identify stocks that effectively hedge climate risk, and I analyze the disclosure’s impact on investors’ equilibrium portfolio choices. I then study firms’ voluntary disclosure incentives and analyze when disclosure mandates enhance risk sharing. Finally, I demonstrate that, by facilitating risk sharing, climate risk disclosure reduces the climate risk premium among stocks held by climate-focused investors. Hence, disclosure can lower the valuations of firms with low climate exposures and the overall market. (JEL: D82, D84, G12, G14)

papers.title: The Horizon of Investors’ Information and Corporate Investment
papers.abstract: The quality of investors’ information across different horizons has real effects. When managers care about the effect of investment on their stock price, a decline in the informativeness of investors’ signals about long-term cash flows leads firms with long-term projects to cut investment more than firms with short-term projects. Using a novel, hand-collected measure of project horizons, we confirm this hypothesis: relative to firms with short-term projects, the investment of firms with long-term projects decreases by 3.7% following a 1-standard-deviation drop in the quality of investors’ long-term information. This effect becomes larger when managers prioritize current stock prices. (JEL D84, G14, G17, M41).

papers.title: The Cross-section of Subjective Expectations: Understanding Prices and Anomalies
papers.abstract: We decompose cross-sectional differences in the level of price-earnings ratios using professional forecasts. High price-earnings ratios are accounted for by both low expected returns and overly high expected earnings growth. The magnitudes and timing of the comovements between prices, earnings growth, and returns are consistent with gradual learning rather than expectations being highly sensitive to recent realizations. Earnings growth surprises do not translate 1-1 into one-period returns but instead are gradually reflected in returns over time. A structural risk-premium model incorporating constant-gain learning about mean earnings growth replicates our findings and generates realistic dispersion and persistence in price-earnings ratios. (JEL G11, G12, G14, G40)

papers.title: Forward Return Expectations
papers.abstract: We measure investors’ short- and long-term stock-return expectations using both options and survey data. These expectations at different horizons reveal what investors think their own short-term expectations will be in the future, or forward return expectations. Across data sources, investors’ forward return expectations are countercyclical, especially when measured as forward risk premiums. This countercyclical variation is, however, excessive, as changes in forward return expectations are too large relative to subsequent realized short-term expectations. The excess variation in forward return expectations can help account for a meaningful share of the stock-price declines during the global financial crisis and the COVID-19 crisis. (JEL G10, G12, G40)

papers.journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
papers.title: Hedging by Giving: Spiritual Insurance and Religious Donations
papers.abstract: We investigate “spiritual insurance”—a mental strategy for coping with risk, where individuals engage in good deeds, including donations, in exchange for perceived blessings and protection. Using bank transactional data, we show that higher income uncertainty and health shocks lead to increased donations, particularly to religious charities. Moreover, individuals who donate to religious charities tend to reduce insurance expenditures. In a field experiment on millions of potential donors through an online platform, we find that spiritual insurance narratives increase giving, providing direct causal evidence for such a motive. Our findings provide new evidence on how spiritual insurance affects household risk-coping behavior.

papers.journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
papers.title: Prospect Theory and Currency Returns: Empirical Evidence
papers.abstract: We empirically investigate the role of prospect theory in the foreign exchange market. A currency-level measure of prospect-theory value, constructed from the historical distribution of exchange rate returns, negatively forecasts future currency excess returns. A long–short strategy based on this measure yields approximately 5% per annum. Predictability is stronger when arbitrage is limited. Bank order flow is positively associated with prospect-theory value, with inter-dealer and proprietary trading primarily driving this relation. Funds trade against prospect-theory value, acting as arbitrageurs. Overall, our findings suggest that investors evaluate currencies based on historical return distributions, consistent with prospect theory.

papers.journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
papers.title: Trended Momentum
papers.abstract: Drawing on cognitive psychology and behavioral theories of pattern recognition and heuristic processing, we offer a new perspective on momentum by highlighting how clear price trends shape investor expectations. Trend clarity (TC) materially strengthens momentum returns: the highest trend-clarity quintile earns annualized returns of 12.68%, compared with 6.90% for a conventional momentum strategy. We also show that TC affects momentum trading intensity within Hong and Stein’s (1999) multiperiod return-chasing model. Additional tests indicate that trading on clear trends is a central feature of momentum, distinct from existing explanations and observable across asset classes and global markets.

papers.journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
papers.title: Countercyclical Risk Aversion: Evidence from 10 Million Auto Insurance Transactions in China
papers.abstract: Whether risk aversion is time-varying and countercyclical is central to modern asset pricing, yet evidence remains limited and is based mainly on experimental, survey, or aggregate stock market data. We provide individual-level evidence from 10 million Chinese auto insurance contracts from 2011 to 2017, estimating policyholders’ risk aversion from deductible choices. We find that risk aversion is time-varying and countercyclical. The estimates are negatively related to lottery and stock trading, positively related to insurance sales and bond trading, and vary with psychological factors, including seasonal mood, “zodiac year,” and calendar events.

papers.journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
papers.title: U.S. Banks’ Exposures to Climate Transition Risks
papers.abstract: We propose a new approach to estimate banks’ credit exposures to transition risks that combines sectoral effects of climate policies from general equilibrium (GE) models with historical information on loans’ default risks. At worst, estimated exposures reach 14% of bank loan portfolio values. Accounting for historic loan payoff structures reduces exposures to 0.5%–2%. Exposures can increase by 3–5 percentage points due to aggregate economic shocks. Analyses surrounding climate transition events suggest our estimates can serve as an upper bound on banks’ transition risk exposures. Highlighting our measure’s novelty, emissions explain at most 60% of variation in banks’ exposures.

papers.journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
papers.title: Are the Hedges of Funds Green?
papers.abstract: Over the past decade, hedge funds have increasingly embraced green investing. We develop a novel return-based measure of fund greenness and find that greener funds earn higher average returns, consistent with capturing a positive green premium, and are associated with lower risks, especially during adverse periods. We further show that performance gains are greatest among directional funds, whereas risk reduction is most pronounced among nondirectional funds. We also provide evidence that managers of these funds exhibit superior green investment skills through green stock selection and green factor timing. Finally, investors reward greener hedge funds only when they demonstrate strong performance.

papers.journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
papers.title: Housing Yields
papers.abstract: We build a granular data set of residential property yields using rental and sale listings from a major German real estate platform. With more than 1.5 million property-level rent-to-price ratios, we document a novel heterogeneity puzzle. About two-fifths of yield dispersion remains unexplained after controlling for extensive observable property characteristics and postal code-level time-varying factors using fixed effects. When we absorb finer neighborhood amenities through richer fixed effects, the unexplained share remains close to one-third. This evidence points to the importance of investors’ beliefs and preferences—rather than several alternative explanations we test—as sources of heterogeneity in risk premia.

papers.journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
papers.title: Economic Fundamentals and Short-Run Exchange Rate Prediction: A Machine-Learning Perspective
papers.abstract: The exchange rate predictability puzzle—that fundamentals fail to forecast short-horizon exchange rate movements out of sample—has long resisted resolution. We show that fundamentals do matter, but their effects vary with global financial conditions. Using a rich set of country characteristics interacted with global state variables and machine-learning techniques to handle the high-dimensional data, we document that interactions between country characteristics and foreign exchange market volatility are particularly important, consistent with a “flight to fundamentals” during periods of financial stress. Our forecasts deliver substantial economic value and offer new insight into the carry trade.

papers.journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
papers.title: Does the Salience of Climate-Related Risk Affect Asset Prices?
papers.abstract: Using regression discontinuity and difference-in-differences designs to compare prices of California homes across a new wildfire risk zone boundary, I identify null effects in the immediate vicinity of the new risk zone boundary. In contrast, prices of homes newly assigned to a riskier zone drop by 5.7% further away from the new risk zone boundary. These findings suggest that households do not respond to the risk salience triggered by the new risk zone assignment. Instead, they update their risk beliefs in response to rezoning in a way that is consistent with the actual wildfire risk.

papers.journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
papers.title: Does Climate Change Affect Firm Sales? Identifying Supply Effects
papers.abstract: We estimate the supply-side effects of climate change on firm sales by exploiting variation in local average temperature across suppliers of the same client. A 1°C increase in temperature leads to a 2.5% decline in annual sales. This effect is nonlinear, with stronger effects among suppliers in regions with the largest temperature increases and in cooler regions. Manufacturing and heat-sensitive industries are more affected, consistent with a reduction in labor productivity and labor supply when local temperatures rise. Nondiversified and financially constrained firms are also more affected, supporting the importance of operational and financial flexibility in adapting to climate change.

papers.journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
papers.title: Market Return Decomposition and Equity Risk Premium Predictability
Programmable Repayment: Risk-Sharing and Enforcement Through the Payment Platform
papers.abstract: Payment platforms increasingly offer merchants loans with programmable repayment, deducting a share of merchants’ platform sales toward repayment. The contract transfers part of merchants’ cash-flow risk to the lender and automates collection, but merchants partly control which sales the platform processes. This puts risk-sharing in tension with enforcement. At a major Indian payment platform, merchants accept offers more often when sales are volatile or outside debts are overdue. After disbursal, borrowers’ platform sales fall 12 percent relative to matched controls. Declines are larger among high-volatility merchants and on second loans, so the deduction base shrinks with borrower risk and experience. These larger declines come without detectably greater outside arrears. Declines are smaller where cash is scarce, consistent with diversion. The lender nevertheless earns 9.6 percent annually before costs, above the 6.5 percent Treasury-bill yield. High-volatility merchants generate comparable loan returns, stay longer on the platform, and contribute more rental revenue.

papers.title: Dangerous Liaisons? Debt Supply and Convenience Yield Spillovers in the Euro Area*
papers.abstract: The literature established that a sovereign bond’s “convenience yield” premium diminishes when that country issues more debt. But how is this convenience yield affected when another country issues sovereign debt? Using high-frequency identification and debt management offices’ communication, we find that an increase in German or French debt reduces convenience yields across the eurozone. Spillovers to low-risk countries are one-for-one while those to riskier countries are smaller. To rationalize these findings, we develop a model with heterogeneous credit risk. Safe sovereign bonds are close substitutes to hedge against idiosyncratic risk, explaining large spillovers, while risky bonds are poor substitutes.

papers.title: Government Guarantees and Dynamic Debt Runs
papers.abstract: This study quantifies the impact of public guarantees on the stability of bank wholesale funding. We study the Chinese market for negotiable certificates of deposit (NCDs) around the first bank failure in two decades, the Baoshang event, which struck investors’ belief in government guarantees on wholesale bank debt. We document a sharp increase in NCD spreads, issuance failures, and runs, with weaker banks becoming more exposed to rollover risk after the event. Using a model of dynamic debt runs, we estimate that the perceived guarantee fell from 54% of creditor losses before the event to approximately zero after the event. The decline is largest for small banks, low-rated banks, and rural commercial banks. Our structural model also allows us to compare alternative policies aimed at stabilizing creditors’ willingness to roll over short-term debt.

papers.title: Large Funds and Corporate Bond Market Fragility
papers.abstract: The corporate bond fund industry is characterized by a high concentration of capital, with a substantial portion of assets managed by large funds. We examine the relation between large-fund trading exposure and corporate bond volatility across market conditions. Using a comprehensive sample of U.S. bond funds and corporate bonds, we show that bond return volatility decreases (increases) with trading fund size when market liquidity is high (low). Exploring the underlying mechanisms, we find that large funds are more likely to reach for yield by holding illiquid bonds. Further analysis suggests that while large funds supply liquidity during normal times, their liquidity-supplying activity weakens during market stress. Finally, large funds tend to sell illiquid bonds when facing investor outflows during illiquid markets. Overall, our findings reveal an important yet subtle relation between fund size and bond market fragility, akin to a “dam effect.” JEL Classification: G10, G12, G23

papers.title: A Conditional Shrinkage Method for Portfolio Selection
papers.abstract: We develop a conditional shrinkage method for portfolio selection. Our approach builds on a decomposition of the mean-variance portfolio into the 1/N portfolio and an alpha component that offers large efficiency gains but is exposed to substantial estimation risk. We show that a linear shrinkage covariance matrix determines the portfolio’s relative exposure to these components, and our framework allows the shrinkage intensity to depend on a state variable that predicts their relative performance. We implement the method using investor sentiment and find that the estimated relation predominantly leads to greater shrinkage toward 1/N when sentiment is low, improving mean-variance efficiency while maintaining low turnover. JEL Classification: G11, G12.

papers.title: The DNA of Neuroticism and Financial Decisions
papers.abstract: A polygenic score (PGS) capturing genetic predisposition toward neuroticism predicts heterogeneity in risk aversion, return beliefs, and stock market participation. This approach addresses key methodological and interpretive concerns associated with phenotypic measures of neuroticism. Risk aversion and return beliefs are important, but incomplete, channels linking the neuroticism PGS to stock market participation. The neuroticism PGS also predicts heterogeneity in demographic and behavioral characteristics previously shown to influence financial choices. These characteristics serve as key channels through which the genetic propensity for neuroticism shapes financial choices.

papers.title: Local Returns and Beliefs about the Stock Market
papers.abstract: We show that investors extrapolate from recent stock returns of locally headquartered firms when forming beliefs about aggregate stock market outcomes. While it may be optimal to rely on local information, these effects are unrelated to how informative local returns are on predictions of aggregate outcomes. Evidence from a sample of retail investors suggests this belief extrapolation is driven by investors’ own holdings of local firms. Our findings suggest that beliefs about information contained in public signals vary systematically with geography, and are an important component of local biases in equity markets.

papers.title: Who Do You Vote For? Same-Race Voting Preferences in Director Elections
papers.abstract: This paper highlights racial and ethnic preferences in corporate director elections. Using a comprehensive dataset of mutual fund voting records, we discover that mutual fund managers are more likely to vote for director nominees who share their racial or ethnic identity. Funds managed by White-dominated teams exhibit the strongest same-race preferences, particularly those in fund families with scarce minority representation. Same-race voting preferences have detrimental implications for the career outcomes of minority director candidates, and are associated with worse fund performance primarily when fund managers operate under weaker accountability. We investigate various potential mechanisms—including statistical discrimination, value maximization, conflicts of interest, social networks, and taste-based biases—and find that the evidence aligns most closely with a taste-based explanation for same-race preferential voting. JEL Classification: G23, G34, G41, J71
